ex.en: The more you practice, the fewer mistakes you make.

연습하다.nuance: 연습하다 is Sino-Korean 練習 — 練 'train/temper (as in tempering metal)' + 習 'repeatedly do/learn' — so 'train by repetition', i.e. drill a skill until it improves. The key contrast is with 공부하다 'to study': 공부하다 is taking in knowledge (grammar, facts, theory), whereas 연습하다 is repeated hands-on doing to build a SKILL — you 공부해 grammar but 연습해 speaking and piano. A closely related word is 훈련하다 (訓練, 'train'), which is more systematic/physical (soldiers, athletes), while 연습하다 is everyday practice. The thing practiced is a direct OBJECT with 을/를: 발음을 연습하다. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: don't say 발음에 연습하다 (no 에), and don't reach for 공부하다 when you mean drilling a skill. As a noun+하다 verb it conjugates on 하다 (연습해요, 연습했어요, formal 연습합니다); negative/impossible split the noun (연습 안 해요, 연습 못 해요).
연습하다.explanation: 연습하다 (yeonseupada) = "to practice". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 연습해요 plus one useful sentence like 발음을 연습하다 ("to practice pronunciation"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 연습하고 싶어요 for what you want, 연습할 수 있어요 for what you can, 연습 못 해요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations.
연습하다.shortExplanation: 연습하다 means "to practice" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 연습하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 연습해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Choosing 공부하다 for skill drills — 'I study speaking every day' as 말하기를 공부해요 sounds off; repeated skill practice is 연습하다: 말하기를 연습해요.
Marking the practiced thing with 에 (발음에 연습해요) — it is a direct object: 발음을 연습해요.
Writing the negative as 안 연습해요 — split it: 연습 안 해요 (impossible = 연습 못 해요).

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 연습하다 becomes 연습할 수 있어요 ("can") and 연습할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

After that the endings carry the meaning — 공부하고 싶어요 for what you want, 공부할 수 있어요 for what you can, 공부 못 해요 for what you can't. 보다.nuance: 보다 covers seeing, watching, and looking at something. Context tells which English verb fits.
보다.explanation: "to see / watch" in Korean is 보다 (boda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 봐요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 보다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 영화를 봐요 ("watch a movie.") — then reshape the same stem into 보고 싶어요 (desire), 볼 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 봐요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
보다.shortExplanation: 보다 means "to see / watch" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 보다 as a complete polite sentence.

커피.nuance: In speech, 커피 마셔요 without 를 is also natural, but learn the full frame first.
커피.explanation: 커피 (keopi) means "coffee". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 커피 주세요 ("Coffee, please."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 커피 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.

음악.nuance: 음악 is Sino-Korean, 音樂 ('sound-pleasure/joy'), and is the general word for music. Its everyday partner verb is 듣다 ('hear/listen'), which is a ㄷ-irregular: before a vowel the ㄷ becomes ㄹ, so 듣 + 어요 → 들어요 and 듣 + 으면 → 들으면 — memorize this because beginners often write the wrong ❌들다. Distinguish 음악 from 노래: 노래 is a specific 'song' you can sing (with words and a tune), while 음악 is music as a whole, including instrumental pieces, so background café music is 음악, not 노래. Two near-verbs differ too — 듣다 is to receive sound, but 틀다 is to switch a track on from a device. The English-speaker pitfall is using 보다 ('watch') because you 'watch a music video' in English; for plain audio say 음악을 들어요, and avoid the false stem 들다 — the dictionary form is 듣다.
음악.explanation: 음악 (eumak) = "music". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 음악을 들어요 ("I listen to music") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 음악, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
음악.shortExplanation: 음악 means "music" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 음악을 봐요 by analogy with watching videos — pure listening uses 듣다, so 음악을 들어요.
Writing the stem as 들다 and conjugating 들어요 from it — the base verb is the ㄷ-irregular 듣다; the ㄹ only appears before a vowel ending.
Using 만들다 for 'make/play music' on a device — to start a track you 틀다, e.g. 음악을 틀어요.

usagePhrases.note: 듣다 'hear/listen' takes 을; note ㄷ→ㄹ in 들어요
좋다 is an adjective; subject marker 이
좋아하다 (verb) governs an object with 을

examples.en: I listen to music.

영화.nuance: 영화 is Sino-Korean, 映畵 ('project-picture'), literally a projected image, and it is the standard word for a movie/film. It pairs with 보다 ('see/watch'), never 듣다 ('listen'), because film is something you view. A single film is counted with the bound noun 편 (영화 두 편 = two movies), not 개. Don't confuse 영화 with 드라마: 드라마 is a serialized TV series, while 영화 is a self-contained cinema film, so a Korean TV soap is a 드라마, not a 영화. The cinema building is 영화관 (or the loanword 극장). The classic English-speaker pitfall is letting 'a movie' steer you to the generic counter 개 (영화 한 개 sounds wrong) — use 편; and don't calque 'go to a movie' as 영화에 가다, since you say 영화(를) 보러 가다, 'go in order to watch a movie'.
영화.explanation: "movie" is 영화 (yeonghwa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 영화를 봐요 ("I watch a movie"). Watch the particle attached to 영화 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
영화.shortExplanation: 영화 means "movie" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 영화를 들어요 by mixing up senses — you don't 'listen to' a film; the verb is 보다, so 영화를 봐요.
Counting with 개 as in 영화 한 개 — films use the dedicated counter 편: 영화 한 편.
Translating 'go to a movie' as 영화에 가요 — Korean expresses purpose, so it is 영화를 보러 가요 ('go to watch a movie').

걷다.nuance: 걷다 means to walk on foot and is a ㄷ irregular verb: before a vowel ending the final ㄷ softens to ㄹ, so the 요-form is 걸어요 (not 걷어요) and the past is 걸었어요. Before a consonant ending the ㄷ stays put, so the formal form remains 걷습니다 and you say 걷지 마세요, 걷고 싶어요. The nearest relative is 산책하다 ('take a stroll'): 걷다 is the raw act of walking anywhere, while 산책하다 implies a leisurely walk for pleasure, so 'I walk to work' is 걸어서 출근해요, never 산책해서 출근해요. The trap for English speakers is that 걷다 doesn't take an object the way 'walk the dog' does — Korean uses 산책시키다 for that, and the path you walk takes 을/를 (공원을 걸어요), so don't reach for 에. Also remember 걸어서 ('on foot') is one fixed chunk for describing how you travel.
걷다.explanation: 걷다 (geotda) means "to walk". Start from the polite form 걸어요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 걷다. A strong first sentence is 공원을 걸어요 ("I walk in/through the park"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 걷다 also becomes 걷고 싶어요 (want), 걸을 수 있어요 (can), and 못 걸어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
걷다.shortExplanation: 걷다 means "to walk" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 걷다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 걸어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Keeping the ㄷ and saying 걷어요/걷었어요 — because 걷다 is a ㄷ irregular, the ㄷ becomes ㄹ before vowels, so the correct forms are 걸어요/걸었어요 (the ㄷ only survives before consonants, as in 걷습니다).
Saying 공원에 걸어요 to mean 'I walk in the park' — the space you walk through is the path/object and takes 을/를, so it must be 공원을 걸어요; 에 would wrongly mark a destination.
Translating 'walk the dog' literally as 개를 걸어요 — 걷다 can't take a creature as its object that way; Korean says 개를 산책시켜요 ('make the dog stroll').

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will

That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem: ㄷ → ㄹ
conjugationTips.body: 걷다 is a ㄷ-irregular verb. The final ㄷ becomes ㄹ before a vowel ending, so it conjugates to 걸어요, never the literal ㄷ + 어요. The ㄷ stays ㄷ before a consonant ending (듣고, 듣습니다).

피곤하다.nuance: 피곤하다 is physical/general tiredness — worn out, drained, exhausted — typically after work, study, travel, or poor sleep. It is Sino-Korean 疲困 (疲 weary + 困 exhausted), literally 'weary-exhausted', which is why it reads as bodily fatigue rather than sleepiness. Keep it apart from 졸리다 ('sleepy'): you can be 피곤하다 yet wide awake (drained but not nodding off), and 졸리다 is specifically wanting to sleep — don't swap them. It is also milder and more everyday than 지치다 ('to be worn out/burned out'), which implies you've reached your limit. As a regular 하다-adjective it is 피곤해요 (not 피곤하요). One common English-speaker slip: 피곤하다 normally describes a PERSON being tired; to call an activity 'tiring' you also use 피곤하다 (피곤한 일 = 'tiring work'), but to call a person 'tiresome/draining' Koreans say 피곤한 사람 — meaning 'a person who is exhausting to deal with', a nuance worth knowing so you don't misread it as 'a tired person.'
피곤하다.explanation: "tired" is 피곤하다 (pigonhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 피곤해요 ("I am tired"). Watch the particle attached to 피곤하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
피곤하다.shortExplanation: 피곤하다 means "tired" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 피곤하요 — 하다 contracts to 해, so it's 피곤해요.
Using 피곤하다 to mean 'sleepy.' Drained-but-awake is 피곤하다; wanting to sleep is 졸리다. 'I'm sleepy' = 졸려요, not 피곤해요.
Assuming 피곤한 사람 always means 'a tired person.' In conversation it often means 'an exhausting/high-maintenance person.' Context decides — be careful when describing someone.

examples.en: Today I'm really tired.
examples.note: 요-form 피곤해요 for your own bodily state

The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 늦다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. 늦다.shortExplanation: 늦다 means "to be late" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 늦게 when the sentence needs 'be late': 늦을 것 같아요, not 늦게 것 같아요.
For a delayed reply, 답장이 늦다 is natural.

usagePhrases.en: I think I will be a little late.
usagePhrases.note: Soft warning before you arrive late.

usagePhrases.en: I guess the reply is late.

examples.en: Traffic is heavy, so I might be a bit late.
examples.note: -ㄹ지도 몰라요 leaves the possibility open.

ex.en: There's a reason, you see. Let me explain.
ex.note: -거든요 introduces the fact of having a reason as new information, then promises the full explanation

이유.nuance: 이유 is Sino-Korean (理由, 理 'principle/logic' + 由 'cause/origin'), the 'reason' or grounds behind something — the answer to 'why?'. Its sharpest contrast is with 원인 (原因, 'cause'): 이유 is the justification or motive a person gives ('the reason I'm late'), often subjective and explainable, while 원인 is the objective, often impersonal cause of a result ('the cause of the fire', 화재의 원인). So you ask a friend 무슨 이유로 늦었어? but an investigator looks for the 원인 of an accident. Also distinguish 까닭, a more native, slightly literary synonym of 이유. Register-neutral and extremely common. Core collocations: 이유가 있다/없다, 이유를 묻다/대다/설명하다, 이유 없이 (for no reason), 그런 이유로 (for that reason), ~는 이유는 (the reason that ~ is). The English-speaker pitfall: don't bolt 이유 onto a 'because' clause redundantly — Korean already has 왜냐하면 ... 때문이에요 / ~기 때문에 to say 'because', so '왜냐하면 그 이유는...' is clunky; pick one. Also, 'the reason is because...' should be ~는 이유는 ... 때문이에요, where the sentence ends in 때문이다, not a second 이유.
이유.explanation: 이유 (iyu) means "reason". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 이유가 있다 ("to have a reason"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 이유 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
이유.shortExplanation: 이유 means "reason" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 원인 for a personal motive — the reason you skipped class is 이유, while 원인 is an objective cause (사고의 원인 = the cause of the accident).
Doubling up 'because': '왜냐하면 그 이유는 비가 와서요' is redundant; say 왜냐하면 비가 왔기 때문이에요, or simply 비가 와서요.
Forgetting 때문이다 closes a 'the reason is...' sentence: 늦은 이유는 차가 막혔기 때문이에요, not 늦은 이유는 차가 막혔어요.

usagePhrases.note: 이유 + 이 with 있다, there exists a reason
이유 + 를 with 묻다, to inquire why
이유 + 없이 forms the adverb 'for no reason'
이유 + 로 with 무슨, asking the grounds 'on what reason'

examples.en: There's no special reason.
examples.note: Simple frame: 이유 + 없다 to brush off a 'why' question politely.

examples.en: Please explain the reason you're late.
examples.note: Everyday frame: [modifier]~(으)ㄴ + 이유 packs the reason into a noun phrase.

examples.ko: 회사를 그만둔 이유는 여러 가지가 있지만, 가장 큰 이유는 건강이었어요.
examples.romanization: hoesareul geumandun iyuneun yeoreo gajiga itjiman, gajang keun iyuneun geongangieosseoyo.
examples.en: There are several reasons I quit the company, but the biggest reason was my health.
examples.note: Real situation: layering reasons (여러 가지 이유 / 가장 큰 이유) when explaining a big decision.

ex.ko: 제 생각에는 이 방법이 더 좋을 것 같아요.
ex.en: In my opinion, I think this method is better.
ex.note: 제 생각에는 = 'in my view' — a standard phrase for introducing soft opinions in conversation

생각.nuance: 생각 is the native Korean catch-all noun for a 'thought', 'idea', or 'opinion' — anything that happens in the mind: memories, intentions, plans, beliefs, judgments. It is far broader and softer than Sino-Korean 의견 (a defined stance for discussion): 좋은 생각이에요 praises an idea, whereas 의견 frames it as a formal position. It also overlaps with 마음 ('heart/mind' as feeling/will), but 생각 is the cognitive 'thinking' side while 마음 is the emotional/volitional side — 생각이 바뀌다 = I changed my mind (reasoning), 마음이 바뀌다 = my heart changed (feelings). Register-neutral and one of the highest-frequency nouns in the language. Key collocations: 생각이 나다 (come to mind/remember), 생각이 들다 (a thought arises), 생각해 보다 (think it over), ~라고 생각하다 (to think that ~). The big English-speaker pitfall is the verb pattern: 'I think that it's true' is 사실이라고 생각해요 with the quotative ~라고, not 사실 생각해요; and 'I remember' is most naturally 생각나요, not a literal translation. Don't confuse 생각나다 (it comes to mind, intransitive) with 생각하다 (to actively think, transitive).
생각.explanation: 생각 (saenggak) = "thought, idea". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 생각이 나다 ("to come to mind / remember") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 생각, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
생각.shortExplanation: 생각 means "thought, idea" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Dropping the quotative ~라고: 'I think it's good' is 좋다고 생각해요, not 좋다 생각해요 or 좋은 것 생각해요.
Mixing up 생각나다 and 생각하다 — 생각나다 = it pops into your head (옛날이 생각나요), 생각하다 = you deliberately think (잘 생각하세요).
Using 생각 for a formal 'opinion' in a meeting where 의견 fits better — 생각 sounds casual/personal, 의견 sounds like a position offered for debate.

usagePhrases.note: 생각 + 이 with 나다, an idea or memory pops up by itself
생각 + 이 with 들다, a thought arises in you
생각 + 을 with 하다, the everyday 'to think things over'
생각 + 이다 evaluates a suggestion as good

examples.en: That's a good idea!
examples.note: Simple frame: 생각 + 이에요 to praise a suggestion someone just made.

examples.en: Yesterday's events suddenly came to mind.
examples.note: Everyday frame: 생각나다 (one written verb) = 'to remember / cross one's mind' on its own.

examples.ko: 며칠 동안 곰곰이 생각해 봤는데, 그냥 포기하는 게 나을 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: myeochil dongan gomgomi saenggakae bwanneunde, geunyang pogihaneun ge naeul geot gatayo.
examples.en: I thought it over carefully for a few days, and I feel it's better to just give up.
examples.note: Real situation: 생각해 보다 (think it over) leading to a tentative conclusion with ~것 같다.

ex.en: Please share your opinion.
ex.note: More formal than 생각 — used in meetings, discussions, and written Korean

의견.nuance: 의견 is Sino-Korean (意見, 意 'mind/intention' + 見 'view/seeing'), literally 'how your mind sees something' — a considered position or judgment you can defend, usually about a topic, plan, or issue. The crucial contrast is with 생각: 생각 is the broad word for any 'thought' that crosses your mind, while 의견 is specifically a stance offered for discussion or evaluation, so a meeting asks for 의견 (positions), not just 생각 (musings). It is register-neutral and very common in school and workplace settings; the polite request 의견을 여쭤봐도 될까요? raises it a notch. Natural collocations: 의견을 말하다/내다/제시하다 (state/put forward), 의견이 다르다/같다 (disagree/agree), 의견을 모으다 (gather opinions), 반대 의견 (an opposing view). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 의견 every time you'd say 'I think' — 'I think it's good' is 좋은 것 같아요 or 좋다고 생각해요, NOT 좋은 의견이에요; 의견 is the opinion itself as a thing, not the act of thinking. Also don't say 의견하다 — there is no such verb; you 의견을 말하다.
의견.explanation: "opinion" is 의견 (uigyeon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 의견을 말하다 ("to state an opinion"). Watch the particle attached to 의견 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
의견.shortExplanation: 의견 means "opinion" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 의견하다 to mean 'to opine' — 의견 is a noun with no verb form; use 의견을 말하다 / 의견을 내다.
Using 의견 where English 'I think...' just hedges — 'I think it'll rain' is 비가 올 것 같아요, not an 의견; 의견 is a stance offered for discussion.
Confusing 의견 with 생각 — 생각 is any thought; 의견 is a position on a topic, so a survey or meeting collects 의견, while daydreaming is 생각.

usagePhrases.note: 의견 + 을 with 말하다, the default verb for voicing a view
의견 + 이 with 다르다, the set way to say 'we disagree'
의견 + 을 with 듣다, asking for input
의견 stands as a count noun you can put 다른 'other' in front of

examples.en: My opinion is a little different.
examples.note: Simple frame: 의견은 + adjective states where you stand on something.

examples.ko: 이 문제에 대해 여러분의 의견을 듣고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: i munjee daehae yeoreobunui uigyeoneul deutgo sipeoyo.
examples.en: I'd like to hear your opinions on this issue.
examples.note: Everyday frame: ~에 대해 (about) + 의견을 듣다, common in class or meetings.

examples.ko: 회의에서 제 의견을 솔직하게 말했지만 받아들여지지 않았어요.
examples.romanization: hoeuieseo je uigyeoneul soljikage malhaetjiman badadeuryeojiji anasseoyo.
examples.en: I gave my opinion frankly in the meeting, but it wasn't accepted.
examples.note: Real situation: voicing 의견 at work, with the realistic outcome that it may be rejected.

ex.ko: 그 강의 진짜 지루한 것 같아요.
ex.en: That lecture seems really boring.
ex.note: Adjective → -(으)ㄴ 것 같다: 지루한 것 같다. Bare 지루해요 would sound like a harsh verdict

지루하다.nuance: 지루하다 is 'boring/tedious' for something that DRAGS — a long meeting, a dull movie, a slow lecture — the quality of an experience that wears your patience thin. This is the mirror image of 심심하다, and keeping them straight is one of the most useful distinctions in this set: 지루하다 describes the boring THING/experience (영화가 지루해 = 'the movie is boring'), while 심심하다 describes a bored PERSON with nothing to do (나는 심심해 = 'I'm bored'). So 'I'm bored' (idle) ≠ 'this is boring' (tedious) — the first is 심심해요, the second 지루해요. As a regular 하다-adjective it is 지루해요 (not 지루하요), modifier 지루한. A near-synonym is 따분하다, which is similar 'dull/tedious' with a slightly more listless, fed-up flavor; 지루하다 is the neutral default. English-speaker pitfall: because English uses one word 'boring/bored' for both the cause and the feeler, learners say 나는 지루해요 meaning 'I'm bored' — but that literally implies 'I am a boring thing.' For your own idle boredom say 심심해요; reserve 지루하다 for the tedious thing itself.
지루하다.explanation: 지루하다 (jiruhada) = "boring". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 지루해요 ("it's boring") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 지루하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
지루하다.shortExplanation: 지루하다 means "boring" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 지루하요 — 하다 contracts to 해, so it's 지루해요.
Saying 나는 지루해요 to mean 'I'm bored (nothing to do).' That reads as 'I am boring.' Use 심심해요 for a bored person; 지루하다 is for a tedious thing/experience.
Mixing 지루하다 and 심심하다 in general. Remember the pair: a dull movie/class = 지루하다 (it drags); a person with empty time = 심심하다 (idle).

usagePhrases.note: the boring thing takes 이/가 as subject

usagePhrases.en: I'm bored to death (it's so dull)

examples.en: This book is a bit boring.
examples.note: 요-form 지루해요 describing a tedious thing

examples.en: The meeting was so long that it got boring.
examples.note: -아서 cause + past 지루했어요

examples.en: If the movie is boring, you can just sleep.
examples.note: -면 'if boring' + 자도 되다 'may sleep'

ex.en: I found it fun, actually. I rather liked it.
ex.note: -거든요: introducing a contrasting opinion the other person didn't know you held — new information to explain your reaction

재미있다.nuance: 재미있다 is literally 재미 (fun, enjoyment) + 있다 (to exist) — 'fun exists [in it]' — which is exactly why it conjugates like 있다 and gives 재미있어요, and why the noun-modifying form is the 있다-style 재미있는 N (재미있는 영화), never 재미있은. It spans both English 'fun' and 'interesting': a party, a game, or a class can all be 재미있어요, so let context choose the English. The near-synonym to separate is 재미있다 vs 흥미롭다: 재미있다 is the warm, everyday 'enjoyable/entertaining' you say about a movie or a friend, while 흥미롭다 is a cooler, more bookish 'intriguing/of interest' you might use for a research finding or a phenomenon — calling a thrilling roller coaster 흥미로워요 sounds oddly academic. Its direct opposite is the single word 재미없다 (재미 + 없다, 'fun does not exist') = boring; do not say 안 재미있다 as your default negative — 재미없어요 is the natural 'it's boring', and 안 재미있어요 reads more like 'it's not [particularly] fun'. The big English-speaker pitfall is the conjugation: because the headword ends in 있다, learners over-apply -하다 or vowel rules and produce 재미있다요 or 재미있아요; the only correct polite form is 재미있어요, with past 재미있었어요.
재미있다.explanation: 재미있다 (jaemiitda) means "to be fun; interesting". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 재미있어요 ("it's fun / interesting"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 재미있다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
재미있다.shortExplanation: 재미있다 means "to be fun; interesting" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 재미있다요 or 재미있아요 — it inherits 있다's pattern, so the polite form is 재미있어요 and the past is 재미있었어요.
Forming the modifier as 재미있은 N. 있다-type stems take -는, so it is 재미있는 영화.
Defaulting to 안 재미있어요 for 'it's boring'. The natural, idiomatic word is the opposite 재미없어요; 안 재미있어요 is weaker and less common.

usagePhrases.note: 있다-type modifier is 재미있는, not 재미있은

examples.en: This game is really fun!
examples.note: casual reaction; 진짜 = 'for real' in speech

examples.en: Studying Korean is fun.
examples.note: the thing judged fun takes 이/가, not 을/를

examples.en: The movie I saw yesterday was fun.
examples.note: past tense 재미있었어요 from 재미있- + -었어요

cluster.title: 재미있다 vs 즐겁다 vs 웃기다
cluster.rule: 재미있다 is the default for anything entertaining or interesting — a movie, a game, a class. 즐겁다 is the pleasant feeling of an activity or time spent together (and the fixed word in wishes like 즐거운 하루 보내세요), while 웃기다 specifically means it makes you laugh.

members.hint: the pleasant feeling of doing something

members.en: to make someone laugh; to be funny

ex.ko: 이 소설은 전개가 느린 것 같아요.
ex.en: I think this novel's pacing is slow.
ex.note: 느리다 is an adjective → 느린 것 같다. 전개 is commonly used in film and book reviews

전개.nuance: Use 전개 for the flow of a story or argument, not for a person's speed.
전개.explanation: 전개 (jeongae) means "development / pacing (of a story)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 전개가 느린 것 같아요. ("I think the pacing is slow."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 전개 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
전개.shortExplanation: 전개 means "development / pacing (of a story)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not translate pacing literally as 속도 in movie-review sentences when you mean story development. 전개 is more natural.

usagePhrases.en: I think the pacing is slow.
usagePhrases.note: 느리다 is an adjective, so use 느린 것 같아요.

examples.en: The pacing is too slow, you know.
examples.note: -잖아요 reminds the listener of something both viewers just experienced.

ex.en: I think the ending was a bit disappointing.
ex.note: 아쉽다 (to feel a lack, to be slightly disappointing) → 아쉬운 것 같다. Softening a criticism with -것 같다 is natural here

결말.nuance: 결말 is about narrative ending; 끝 is more general and less review-like.
결말.explanation: "ending / conclusion (of a story)" is 결말 (gyeolmal). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 결말이 좀 아쉬운 것 같아요. ("I think the ending is a bit disappointing."). Watch the particle attached to 결말 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
결말.shortExplanation: 결말 means "ending / conclusion (of a story)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not overuse 끝 for movie-review nuance. 결말 sounds more natural for story endings.

usagePhrases.en: I think the ending is a bit disappointing.
usagePhrases.note: 아쉽다 becomes 아쉬운 before 것 같아요.

examples.en: I thought the ending felt a bit rushed.
examples.note: Past impression: 것 같았어요.

ex.ko: 그 배우 연기 정말 잘하거든요. 꼭 봐 보세요.
ex.en: That actor is genuinely great at acting, you see. Definitely watch it.
ex.note: -거든요 here shares a personal assessment as new information, then follows up with a recommendation

배우.nuance: 배우 is 俳優 (both 俳 and 優 historically meant 'performer/entertainer'), an old Sino-Korean compound that already covers actors of any gender in film, TV drama, and theater — so there is no need to mark gender, and the English loan 액터 is essentially never used in normal speech. The thing an actor does is 연기 'acting' (연기를 하다 / 연기를 잘하다), not '배우를 하다'; that 연기 vs 배우 split (craft vs person) mirrors 요리 vs 요리사 and trips learners up. Distinguish 배우 from 가수 'singer', 개그맨/코미디언 'comedian', and the broader 연예인 'celebrity/entertainer', which includes all of them. The verb 나오다 ('come out') is the idiomatic way to say an actor 'appears in' a film or show. After the vowel, the copula is 배우예요, and one 배우가 된다.
배우.explanation: 배우 (baeu) = "actor". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 연기를 하다 ("act / perform") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 배우, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.
배우.shortExplanation: 배우 means "actor" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Adding a gender word like 남자배우/여자배우 when it is unnecessary; 배우 alone already covers everyone unless gender is genuinely the point.
Saying 배우를 하다 for 'to act'; the activity is 연기, so use 연기를 하다 or 연기를 잘하다.
Confusing 배우 (actor) with the wider 연예인 (any entertainer/celebrity), which also includes singers and comedians.

usagePhrases.note: the craft is 연기 'acting'; 하다 pairs with it
나오다 'come out/appear'; 에 marks the work it appears in
goal of becoming marked with 가

examples.en: I am an actor.
examples.note: 예요 after the vowel-final 배우

examples.en: That actor acts really well.
examples.note: 연기를 잘하다 'be good at acting' is the set phrase

examples.ko: 이 드라마에는 유명한 배우들이 많이 나와요.
examples.romanization: i deuramaeneun yumyeonghan baeudeuri mani nawayo.
examples.en: Many famous actors appear in this drama.
examples.note: 나오다 'appear'; 들 pluralizes 배우

ex.en: The acting seems natural.
ex.note: 자연스럽다 (to be natural) → irregular: 자연스러운 것 같다. The ㅂ irregular applies here

연기.nuance: 연기 is the noun; 연기하다 is the verb 'to act/perform.'
연기.explanation: 연기 (yeongi) = "acting / performance". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 연기가 자연스러운 것 같아요. ("I think the acting seems natural.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 연기, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
연기.shortExplanation: 연기 means "acting / performance" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not confuse 연기 'acting' with 연기 'smoke' in other contexts; movie/drama context makes the meaning clear.

usagePhrases.en: I think the acting seems natural.

examples.en: The actors' performances were really good, you know.
examples.note: -잖아요 works because both people saw the same acting.

아쉽다.en: to feel a slight lack, to be a (gentle) disappointment

ex.en: I think the end was a bit unsatisfying.
ex.note: ㅂ irregular adjective: 아쉽다 → 아쉬운 것 같다. This exact phrase is very common in Korean reviews and casual talk

아쉽다.nuance: 아쉽다 is mild, wistful regret — 'that's a shame / I wish it were otherwise' — the feeling when something nice didn't happen, ended too soon, or fell just short. It's soft; it's NOT deep sadness. The variant ladder: 아쉽다/아쉬워 (casual) → 아쉬워요 (polite) → 아쉽네(요) (in-the-moment reaction to news) → 좀 아쉽다 (softened, noting a small lack). Note the conjugation: 아쉽다 is a -ㅂ irregular adjective, so the polite stem is 아쉬워요 (아쉽+어요 → 아쉬워요), never 아쉽어요. The dividing line against 슬프다 and 속상하다: 아쉽다 is a gentle 'aw, too bad' about a missed chance or something pleasant ending; 슬프다 is real sadness (loss, grief); 속상하다 is being genuinely hurt or upset inside (frustration, heartache). Sold-out tickets → 아쉽다; a pet dying → 슬프다; your work criticized unfairly → 속상하다. 아쉽다 also covers the sense of 'feeling a lack / something's missing' (뭔가 아쉽다 'something feels lacking'), so context decides. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 슬프다 for everyday letdowns — to a Korean ear that's melodramatic.
아쉽다.explanation: 아쉽다 (aswipda) = "That's a shame / too bad / I wish it were different — mild regret or disappointment.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 아쉽다 ("that's a shame"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.
아쉽다.shortExplanation: 아쉽다 is a practical expression meaning "That's a shame / too bad / I wish it were different — mild regret or disappointment.".
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 슬프다 ('sad') for small letdowns like a canceled plan — that sounds melodramatic; the natural word for mild regret is 아쉽다.
Confusing 아쉽다 with 아깝다 — 아깝다 is 'what a waste / too good to waste' (about value/resources), while 아쉽다 is 'a shame, wish it were otherwise' (about a missed chance).
Conjugating the -ㅂ irregular adjective wrong: the polite form is 아쉬워요 (아쉽+어요 → 아쉬워요), not 아쉽어요.

usagePhrases.note: casual with -네 reacting in the moment

usagePhrases.en: it's a bit of a letdown
usagePhrases.note: with 좀 to soften it further

examples.ko: A: 표 다 팔렸대 / B: 아쉽다.
examples.romanization: A: pyo da pallyeotdae / B: aswipda.
examples.en: A: The tickets are all sold out / B: That's a shame.
examples.note: the bare reaction — light disappointment; 아쉽다 is exactly right for a small letdown, not 슬프다

examples.ko: A: 저 다음 주에 이사 가요 / B: 아, 아쉬워요. 자주 봤는데.
examples.romanization: A: jeo daeum jue isa gayo / B: a, aswiwoyo. jaju bwanneunde.
examples.en: A: I'm moving next week / B: Oh, that's too bad. We saw each other so often.
examples.note: everyday: polite 아쉬워요 expressing regret at parting; the follow-up 자주 봤는데 explains WHY it's a shame

examples.ko: A: 비 와서 소풍 취소됐어 / B: 아쉽다. 날씨만 좋았어도.
examples.romanization: A: bi waseo sopung chwisodwaesseo / B: aswipda. nalssiman joasseodo.
examples.en: A: The picnic got canceled because of rain / B: What a shame. If only the weather had held.
examples.note: real situation: 아쉽다 paired with a wistful -았/었어도 conditional ('if only X') — this is a very natural 아쉽다 follow-up pattern

ex.en: The protagonist seems a bit too perfect.
ex.note: 완벽하다 (to be perfect) → 완벽한 것 같다. Common critique in drama reviews

주인공.nuance: 주인공 can refer to a fictional main character or the lead person in a real event.
주인공.explanation: 주인공 (juingong) means "main character / protagonist". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 주인공 배우가 정말 잘하거든요. ("The lead actor is really good, you see."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 주인공 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
주인공.shortExplanation: 주인공 means "main character / protagonist" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 배우 when you mean the character inside the story; use 주인공 for protagonist, 배우 for actor.

usagePhrases.en: The lead actor is really good, you see.
usagePhrases.note: -거든요 gives this as supporting background for the speaker's opinion.

examples.en: I think the main character is too perfect.
examples.note: 완벽하다 becomes 완벽한 before 것 같아요.

ex.ko: 그 인물한테 공감하기 어려운 것 같아요.
ex.en: I think it's hard to relate to that character.
ex.note: 공감하기 어렵다 = 'it's hard to empathize' — the -기 turns 공감하다 into a noun, then 어렵다 (hard) applies → 어려운 것 같다

ex.ko: 개인적으로는 이 영화가 좀 과대평가된 것 같아요.
ex.en: Personally, I think this movie is a bit overrated.
ex.note: 개인적으로 + -것 같다 is a double-hedging strategy very common in Korean — softens with both 'personally' and 'seems'

개인적으로.nuance: 개인적으로 does not mean privately here; it marks a personal opinion.
개인적으로.explanation: "personally / in my personal opinion" is 개인적으로 (gaeinjeogeuro). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 개인적으로는 열린 결말을 좋아하거든요. ("Personally, I like open endings, you see."). Watch the particle attached to 개인적으로 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
개인적으로.shortExplanation: 개인적으로 means "personally / in my personal opinion" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not combine 개인적으로는 저는 unless you need strong contrast. Usually 개인적으로는 alone is enough.

usagePhrases.en: Personally, I like open endings, you see.
usagePhrases.note: A natural way to explain a different preference without sounding confrontational.

examples.en: Personally, I think it's a bit disappointing.
examples.note: Double softening: personally + seems.

ex.en: To be honest, I was a bit disappointed, you see.
ex.note: -거든요 after an honest admission: the speaker is sharing the real reason/feeling the listener may not have guessed

솔직히.nuance: 솔직히 is more direct than 개인적으로, so pair it with softer grammar when criticizing.
솔직히.explanation: 솔직히 (soljiki) = "honestly / frankly". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 솔직히 좀 아쉬웠거든요. ("Honestly, I was a bit disappointed, you see.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 솔직히, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
솔직히.shortExplanation: 솔직히 means "honestly / frankly" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 솔직히 as a license to be blunt; Korean still often needs softening after it.

usagePhrases.en: Honestly, I was a bit disappointed, you see.
usagePhrases.note: -거든요 gives the honest feeling as background.

examples.ko: 솔직히 말하면 결말이 급한 것 같았어요.
examples.romanization: soljiki malhamyeon gyeolmari geupan geot gatasseoyo.
examples.en: Honestly, I thought the ending felt rushed.
examples.note: 솔직히 말하면 + 것 같았어요 softens a direct critique.

ex.en: It seems everyone evaluates it differently.
ex.note: Verb → -는 것 같다: 평가하는 것 같다. Using this form for a general observation about people in general is very natural

평가하다.nuance: 평가하다 means to evaluate, assess, or rate the value of something — work, performance, art, or even a person (評 'judge/criticize' + 價 'price/value', literally 'to price-judge'). That 價 'value' core is why it feels measured and official, the word on report cards, performance reviews, and product reviews. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 평가해요. With 높게/좋게 평가하다 it means 'to think highly of', and 낮게 평가하다 means 'to underrate' — note these always need the ADVERB (높게), a spot English speakers trip on by reaching for 높은. The synonym line to hold is 평가하다 vs 판단하다: 평가하다 weighs worth on a scale (high/low, good/bad), while 판단하다 reaches a yes/no decision about a situation. Because 평가하다 can sound like you are sitting in judgment, Koreans soften it when appraising people directly, or switch to 판단하다.
평가하다.explanation: 평가하다 (pyeonggahada) = "to evaluate". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 평가해요 plus one useful sentence like 성과를 평가하다 ("to evaluate performance"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 평가하고 싶어요 for what you want, 평가할 수 있어요 for what you can, 평가할 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
평가하다.shortExplanation: 평가하다 means "to evaluate" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 평가하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 평가해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing 평가하요 instead of the contracted 평가해요.
Saying 높은 평가해요 for 'rate highly' — it must be the adverb: 높게 평가해요.
Using 평가하다 to mean 'judge a person harshly' in casual talk; it sounds cold, so 판단하다 or a softened phrasing fits better.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 평가하다 becomes 평가할 수 있어요 ("can") and 평가할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: Standard workplace frame: object + 를 + 평가하다 for appraisals.

examples.en: How do you rate that movie?
examples.note: 어떻게 평가해요? is the everyday way to ask for someone's assessment.

examples.en: The teacher evaluated the students' presentations
examples.note: Grading context; 발표를 평가했어요 with the plain past.

examples.en: Don't judge people only by their appearance
examples.note: 겉모습으로만 = 'by appearance alone'; 으로 marks the basis of judgment.

기대하다.en: to expect, to look forward to

ex.en: I had high expectations, so I was a bit let down, you see.
ex.note: -거든요 again here: explaining personal background (had expectations) that the listener didn't know — this is why the disappointment makes sense

기대하다.nuance: 기대하다 is 期待(기대, 'period-await', i.e. 'await a hoped-for time') + 하다, and unlike English 'expect' it leans positive: it means to anticipate something good and look forward to it. The thing awaited takes 을/를 (여행을 기대해요). Its hugely common intransitive twin 기대되다/기대가 되다 ('to be exciting, to be looked forward to') describes the feeling welling up in you — 내일이 기대돼요 — and beginners must keep the two apart: you 기대하다 a thing, but a thing/situation 기대된다 to you. Contrast with 기다리다 ('wait'), which is just neutral temporal waiting with no hope ('버스를 기다려요'); and with 바라다 ('wish/hope') which is a desire without the sense of confident anticipation. As a 하다 verb: 기대해요 / 기대했어요. The pitfall: English speakers map 'expect' onto neutral or negative situations ('I expect rain', 'I expect you to be late') — Korean 기대하다 cannot carry that. For neutral prediction use 예상하다 (豫想); 기대하다 is only for things you hope will be good.
기대하다.explanation: 기대하다 (gidaehada) means "to expect". Start from the polite form 기대해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 기대하다. A strong first sentence is 여행을 기대하다 ("to look forward to a trip"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 기대하다 also becomes 기대하고 싶어요 (want), 기대할 수 있어요 (can), and 기대할 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
기대하다.shortExplanation: 기대하다 means "to expect" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 기대하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 기대해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 기대하다 for neutral or bad predictions like 'I expect it to rain'. That is 예상하다 (비가 올 것으로 예상해요). 기대하다 is positive anticipation only.
Confusing active 기대하다 with intransitive 기대되다. You 기대하다 something (여행을 기대해요), but a thing 기대된다 to you (여행이 기대돼요) — don't say 여행을 기대돼요.
Treating it as 기다리다. 'I'm waiting for the bus' is 버스를 기다려요 (neutral waiting), whereas 기대하다 adds hopeful excitement and can't replace it.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 기대하다 becomes 기대할 수 있어요 ("can") and 기대할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.en: to look forward to a trip
usagePhrases.note: Object + 을/를 + 기대하다 for the happy-anticipation sense.

examples.en: I'm looking forward to the weekend
examples.note: Plain frame; the hopeful, positive flavor of the verb.

examples.en: I'm really excited for this movie
examples.note: 기대돼요 (from 기대되다) describes the feeling rising in you, no object needed.

examples.en: If you expect too much, you might be disappointed
examples.note: 기대하면 ('if you expect') + 실망하다 pairs hope with its risk.

cluster.title: 기다리다 vs 기대하다
cluster.rule: These are false friends for English "wait for / expect." 기다리다 is actual waiting — time passing until someone or something arrives. 기대하다 is looking forward to something good, with no waiting around involved.

members.when: waiting for a person, bus, turn

example.en: I'm looking forward to the trip.

ex.ko: 이 드라마 추천할 만한 것 같아요.
ex.en: I think this drama is worth recommending.
ex.note: 추천할 만하다 = 'worth recommending' → 추천할 만한 것 같다. The -(으)ㄹ 만한 것 같다 construction softens a recommendation

추천하다.nuance: 추천하다 is neutral and practical. In speech, 추천해 주세요 is much more useful than the dictionary form.
추천하다.explanation: "to recommend" is 추천하다 (chucheonhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 추천해 주세요. ("Please recommend one."). Watch the particle attached to 추천하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.
추천하다.shortExplanation: 추천하다 means "to recommend" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 추천하다 alone as a request. Say 추천해 주세요.
The recommended item usually takes 을/를: 식당을 추천하다, 색을 추천하다.

examples.en: Please recommend another color too.
examples.note: Useful in shopping after trying something on.

ex.en: I think our society is changing rapidly.
ex.note: 다고 생각해요 = 'I think that...' — reported-thought structure using the same 다고 pattern

사회.nuance: 사회 (社會, 社 'community/shrine-group' + 會 'gathering') means 'society' as the whole body of people living together, and as a noun-modifier it stacks directly: 현대 사회, 사회 문제, 사회 복지. The trap for English speakers is 사회생활: it does NOT mean 'social life / hanging out', but working life and managing adult/workplace relationships, so 사회생활을 잘하다 praises someone for handling colleagues and obligations well. Contrast 사회 with 모임 — a 모임 is one concrete small gathering (study group, dinner club), while 사회 is the abstract collective; never use 사회 for 'a get-together'. The particle to learn is 에 for location-of-existence (사회에 문제가 있다), not 에서, when you simply say something exists in society.
사회.explanation: 사회 (sahoe) = "society". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 현대 사회 ("modern society") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 사회, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
사회.shortExplanation: 사회 means "society" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Reading 사회생활 as 'social life / partying'. It almost always means working life and getting along at work, so '제 사회생활이 바빠요' implies a busy professional/adult life, not a busy party schedule.
Using 사회 for a small social gathering ('let's have a 사회 this weekend'). 사회 is the abstract collective; for a get-together use 모임 (모임이 있어요).

usagePhrases.note: 현대 attaches directly with no 의; this is the single most common frame 사회 appears in.
Compound noun used constantly in news and essays; note no spacing change, just 사회 + 문제.

usagePhrases.en: working life / getting along in the adult world
usagePhrases.note: Written as one word; means workplace and adult social duties, NOT 'social life' in the party sense.

usagePhrases.en: to go out into society (e.g., after graduating)
usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the destination; idiom for entering the workforce and adult world.

examples.en: There are many problems in our society.
examples.note: Simple frame: 사회 takes 에 + 는 for 'in (our) society', the location-of-existence particle.

examples.en: Once you graduate from university, you really start your working life.
examples.note: Here 사회생활 = professional/adult life — the everyday meaning a learner must internalize.

examples.ko: 인터넷이 우리 사회를 크게 바꿔 놓았어요.
examples.romanization: inteonesi uri sahoereul keuge bakkwo noasseoyo.
examples.en: The internet has greatly changed our society.
examples.note: 바꿔 놓다 = 'changed it (and it stays that way)'; the lingering-result auxiliary, natural with 사회.

ex.en: My friend said Korean culture is interesting.
ex.note: 재미있다 is 있다-type → add -다고 directly (adjective rule), not -(느)ㄴ다고

문화.nuance: 문화 means 'culture' in the broad sense — the customs, arts, food, and shared ways of life of a group. It is Sino-Korean, 文化 ('writing/civilization' 文 + 'become/transform' 化), literally 'becoming civilized', so it leans toward the refined, collective sense of culture rather than one person's habits. The nearest trap-word is 문학 文學 (literature): the two look and sound almost identical, but 학 'study' vs 화 'transform' completely changes the meaning, so an English speaker who half-hears the word can easily swap them. 문화 also is NOT used for bacterial 'culture' (that is 배양) or for being a 'cultured/refined person' (that is 교양 있다). It loves to form compounds — 대중문화 (pop culture), 문화재 (cultural heritage), 문화생활 (cultural life/leisure) — and the habitual verb is 경험하다 (to experience), as in 다른 문화를 경험하다. The everyday phrase 문화 차이 (cultural difference) is how Koreans tactfully explain awkward moments. Register is neutral, fine in both casual chat and formal writing.
문화.explanation: 문화 (munhwa) = "culture". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 한국 문화 ("Korean culture") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 문화, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
문화.shortExplanation: 문화 means "culture" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Confusing 문화 (culture, 文化) with 문학 (literature, 文學). They differ by one syllable (화 vs 학); saying 한국 문학에 관심이 있어요 means 'interested in Korean literature', not culture. Listen for 화 'transform' vs 학 'study'.
Using 틀리다 to say cultures 'are different': 나라마다 문화가 틀려요 literally means each culture is 'wrong'. The correct verb is 다르다 → 문화가 달라요. 틀리다 = incorrect; 다르다 = different.
Adding a particle inside the compound: writing 한국의 문화 sounds stiff and over-literal in speech. Natural spoken Korean drops it — 한국 문화 — treating the two nouns as one unit.

usagePhrases.note: country name + 문화, no particle between them — it reads as one compound noun
문화 + 차이; this is the standard phrase for the gap between two cultures, e.g. 문화 차이 때문에 (because of cultural difference)
문화 + 를 + 경험하다; 경험하다 (to experience firsthand) is the habitual partner verb, stronger than just 보다
전통 + 문화; often written as one word 전통문화, contrasted with 대중문화 (pop culture)

examples.en: I like Korean culture.
examples.note: Simplest frame: 문화 as a plain object with 를. Notice 한국 문화 sits together with no particle inside it.

examples.en: Culture differs a little from country to country.
examples.note: 나라마다 = 'every country / from country to country'; 문화가 달라요 is the everyday way to say cultures differ — 다르다, not 틀리다.

examples.ko: 외국에서 살면 처음에는 문화 차이 때문에 힘들 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: oegugeseo salmyeon cheoeumeneun munhwa chai ttaemune himdeul su isseoyo.
examples.en: When you live abroad, at first it can be hard because of cultural differences.
examples.note: Real-situation register: 문화 차이 때문에 (because of cultural difference) is the exact phrase Koreans reach for to explain culture shock politely.

ex.ko: 이 마을은 오래된 전통을 그대로 이어 가고 있어요.
ex.en: This village is carrying on its old traditions just as they are.
ex.note: 이어 가다 = keep carrying on; present progressive 가고 있어요 emphasizes the ongoing nature

전통.nuance: 전통 (傳統, 傳 'hand down/pass on' + 統 'lineage/unbroken line') is a custom, value, or practice passed down across generations, and the hanja literally pictures an unbroken line being handed on — which is why it carries a respectful, valued tone. Contrast it sharply with 습관 (習慣, 'habit'): 전통 is shared and inherited by a group, while 습관 is one individual's repeated personal routine (제 습관, never 제 전통). For the descriptive 'it is traditional', you must switch to the adjective 전통적이다 → 전통적인 + noun; 전통 alone is the abstract noun. The classic 직역 trap is time-length: English 'a long tradition' tempts 긴 전통, but Korean fixes this as 오랜 전통, because 오랜 expresses depth in time while 긴 means physically long.
전통.explanation: 전통 (jeontong) means "tradition". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 전통 문화 ("traditional culture"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 전통 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
전통.shortExplanation: 전통 means "tradition" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 긴 전통 for 'a long tradition'. 긴 describes physical length; for time-depth Korean uses the fixed form 오랜 전통.
Confusing 전통 with 습관. 전통 is a group's inherited custom; 습관 is one person's repeated routine — '아침에 운동하는 건 제 습관이에요', not 제 전통.

usagePhrases.note: 전통 modifies the next noun attributively with no 의: 전통 문화, 전통 음식, 전통 시장.
지키다 ('protect, keep') is the default verb; you guard a tradition the way you guard a promise.
Adjective form: 전통적인 + noun (전통적인 결혼식 = a traditional wedding).
오랜 ('longtime') is the fixed modifier for time-depth here, never 긴 ('long' in length).

examples.en: This food is our traditional food.
examples.note: Simplest use: 전통 sits straight in front of 음식 with no particle between them.

examples.ko: 이 마을은 오래된 전통을 그대로 이어 가고 있어요.
examples.romanization: i maeureun oraedoen jeontongeul geudaero ieo gago isseoyo.
examples.en: This village is carrying on its old traditions just as they are.
examples.note: 이어 가다 = 'carry on / continue (and keep going)'; the habitual collocation with 전통.

examples.ko: 저는 전통적인 음악보다 현대 음악을 더 좋아해요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun jeontongjeogin eumakboda hyeondae eumageul deo joahaeyo.
examples.en: I like modern music more than traditional music.
examples.note: Real preference talk: 전통적인 (adjective) modifies 음악, paired against 현대 in a A보다 B 더 frame.

ex.ko: 선생님이 한국 역사가 아주 깊다고 하셨어요.
ex.en: The teacher said Korean history is very deep.
ex.note: 깊다 is an adjective → 깊다고 (plain adjective form + 다고). Teacher gets 하셨어요.

역사.nuance: 역사 means history — both the school subject and the actual record of the past — written 歷史 (歷 'to pass through / experience' + 史 'chronicle, records'), literally 'the record of what has passed'. Distinguish it sharply from 옛날, which is the storytelling adverbial 'long ago / once upon a time': you study 역사 in class, but a folktale starts 옛날 옛적에. It also differs from 역사학, the academic 'study OF history' a scholar specializes in; the everyday school subject is plain 역사. A country's history stacks the country name bare in front — 한국 역사, 세계 역사 — with no 의 needed. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 옛날 or 과거 ('the past') when naming the class; the subject and the discipline are both 역사.
역사.explanation: 역사 (yeoksa) = "history". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 역사를 배워요 ("learn history") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 역사, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.
역사.shortExplanation: 역사 means "history" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 옛날 for the school subject (옛날을 배워요); 옛날 means 'long ago', so the subject is 역사를 배워요.
Saying 역사를 길어요; 길다 is descriptive, so use the subject marker: 역사가 길어요.
Adding 의 in 한국의 역사 by reflex; natural everyday Korean stacks them bare as 한국 역사.

usagePhrases.note: 배우다 takes the object marker 를
길다 is descriptive, so 역사 takes 가
country name 한국 modifies 역사 with no particle
좋아하다 takes the object marker 를

examples.en: I like history.
examples.note: simple: 좋아하다 needs the object marker 를

examples.en: Korean history is very long.
examples.note: 한국 역사 is the topic (는); 길다 describes it

examples.ko: 역사 시험 때문에 어젯밤에 늦게까지 공부했어요.
examples.romanization: yeoksa siheom ttaemune eojetbame neutgekkaji gongbuhaesseoyo.
examples.en: Because of the history exam I studied late last night.
examples.note: real life: 때문에 = 'because of', 늦게까지 = 'until late'

ex.en: The news said the economy is getting increasingly difficult.
ex.note: 어려워지다 has vowel stem 어려워지- → ㄴ다고: 어려워진다고

경제.nuance: 경제 (經濟, 經 'manage/govern' + 濟 'aid/relieve' — from 經世濟民 'govern the world and relieve the people') means 'the economy' as a system. The biggest learner trap is the adjective 경제적이다, which splits into TWO everyday meanings: (1) 'economical', i.e. money-saving (버스가 더 경제적이에요), and (2) 'economic/financial' (경제적 부담 = financial burden) — context decides which. Equally important is the slump idiom: to say the economy is doing badly, Korean uses 경제가 어렵다 or 경제가 안 좋다, NOT a literal 경제가 나쁘다, because 어렵다 ('hard, strained') is the conventional collocation. Keep 경제 (the system/field) distinct from 경영 (經營, business management of a company); they look similar but 경영 is running a firm.
경제.explanation: 경제 (gyeongje) = "economy". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 경제가 어렵다 ("the economy is bad / struggling") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 경제, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
경제.shortExplanation: 경제 means "economy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Translating 'the economy is bad' word-for-word as 경제가 나쁘다. Natural Korean is 경제가 어렵다 or 경제가 안 좋다.
Forgetting that 경제적이다 can mean 'economical (saves money)', so '이게 더 경제적이에요' means 'this is cheaper/more cost-effective', not 'this is more economic'.

usagePhrases.note: 어렵다 (lit. 'difficult') is the idiomatic way to say the economy is in a slump, not 나쁘다.
Standard compound (성장 = growth); 경제 성장률 = the economic growth rate.
Two senses: 'economical (cheap)' and 'economic/financial' (경제적 부담 = financial burden).
경제 takes scope modifiers directly: 세계 경제, 한국 경제, 지역 경제.

examples.en: The economy is tough these days.
examples.note: Plain version of the key idiom: 경제가 어렵다 = 'the economy is struggling', using 어렵다 not 나쁘다.

examples.ko: 정부는 경제 성장을 위해 여러 정책을 내놓았어요.
examples.romanization: jeongbuneun gyeongje seongjangeul wihae yeoreo jeongchaegeul naenoasseoyo.
examples.en: The government put forward various policies for economic growth.
examples.note: 경제 성장을 위해 = 'for economic growth'; 내놓다 = 'put forward (a plan/policy)'.

examples.en: Using public transportation is much more economical.
examples.note: Here 경제적이다 = 'economical / cost-saving' — the everyday wallet-friendly sense, not 'economic'.

ex.en: My friend said he has no interest in politics.
ex.note: 없다 → add -다고 directly (없다고). 없다 is in the same category as 있다 — add -다고, not -는다고.

정치.nuance: 정치 (政治, 政 'governing' + 治 'rule/manage' — literally 'governing and ordering [a state]') is the abstract field and activity of politics. Hold three related words apart: 정치 is the field, 정부 (government) is the concrete body, and 정치인 is an individual politician — so 'a politician' is 정치인/정치가, never the literal 정치 사람. The adjective 정치적이다 labels something 'political', usually with an undertone of being calculated, partisan, or socially sensitive. The particle pitfall is interest: 'interested in politics' is 정치에 관심이 있다 (topic marked with 에), not 정치를 관심이 있다. Culturally, 정치 is treated as a touchy subject, so 정치적인 이야기 is something many Koreans deliberately avoid in polite company.
정치.explanation: "politics" is 정치 (jeongchi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 정치에 관심이 있다 ("to be interested in politics"). Watch the particle attached to 정치 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
정치.shortExplanation: 정치 means "politics" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing up 정치 and 정부. 정치 is the activity/field (정치에 관심이 있다); 정부 is the institution (정부가 발표하다).
Saying 정치 사람 for 'politician'. The correct word is 정치인 (or 정치가); 정치 사람 is not idiomatic Korean.

usagePhrases.note: 관심이 있다/없다 takes 에 on the topic: 정치에 관심이 있다 — never 정치를 관심.
정치 + 인 (person) = a person in politics; 정치가 is a near-equivalent.
Adjective form: 정치적인 문제 = a political issue (often with a sensitive/calculated undertone).

usagePhrases.en: to go into / be active in politics
usagePhrases.note: 하다 here means working in the political arena, e.g. running for office.

examples.en: I'm not interested in politics.
examples.note: Bedrock pattern: interest in a topic is X에 관심이 있다/없다, so 정치 takes 에 here.

examples.ko: 요즘 정치 뉴스를 보면 답답할 때가 많아요.
examples.romanization: yojeum jeongchi nyuseureul bomyeon dapdapal ttaega manayo.
examples.en: These days, watching political news often feels frustrating.
examples.note: 정치 뉴스 = 'political news'; 답답하다 = 'stifling/frustrating', a very Korean emotion word.

examples.ko: 그 문제는 너무 정치적이라서 이야기하기 조심스러워요.
examples.romanization: geu munjeneun neomu jeongchijeogiraseo iyagihagi josimseureowoyo.
examples.en: That issue is too political, so I'm careful about discussing it.
examples.note: 정치적이라서 = adjective + 라서 ('because it is…'); shows the cautious tone Koreans attach to 정치.

ex.en: Experts warned that the environment is gradually getting worse.
ex.note: 나빠지다 (vowel stem 나빠지-) → ㄴ다고: 나빠진다고. 경고했어요 = warned.

환경.nuance: 환경 is Sino-Korean 環境 ('ring/encircle' 環 + 'boundary' 境), literally the boundary that rings you — hence it covers BOTH the natural environment (nature, pollution, climate) and the human conditions around a person: 근무 환경 (work environment), 가정 환경 (home background). The near-synonym 주변(周邊) means the physical 'surroundings/vicinity' you can point at, while 환경 is the abstract set of conditions that shape you, so a noisy 주변 creates a bad 환경. Register is neutral and works in essays, news, and speech alike; it collocates with 보호하다 (protect), 오염되다 (be polluted), and 파괴하다 (destroy). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: say 환경이 좋다 ('the environment is good') or 환경에 좋다 ('good FOR the environment'), never 환경을 좋다 — 좋다 is an adjective and can't take 을/를.
환경.explanation: "environment; surroundings" is 환경 (hwangyeong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 환경을 보호하다 ("to protect the environment"). Watch the particle attached to 환경 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
환경.shortExplanation: 환경 means "environment; surroundings" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 환경 only for nature — it equally means general conditions/surroundings, as in 근무 환경 or 주변 환경; restricting it loses half its range.
Saying 환경을 좋다 — 좋다 is a descriptive adjective, so use 환경이 좋다 (the environment is good) or 환경에 좋다 (good for the environment).
Swapping in 주변 for the abstract sense — 주변 is the visible vicinity, while the set of life conditions is 환경 (가정 환경, not 가정 주변).

usagePhrases.note: 보호하다 (保護, 'guard and protect') is the fixed eco verb, never 지키다 alone here.
Shows the non-nature sense: the conditions around you at work.

usagePhrases.en: to be good for the environment
usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the thing affected; 환경이 좋다 instead means the place itself is nice.

examples.en: I'm very interested in the environment.
examples.note: Simple 관심이 많다 = to have much interest; 에 marks the topic of interest.

examples.ko: 일회용품을 줄이면 환경을 보호할 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: ilhoeyongpumeul jurimyeon hwangyeongeul bohohal su isseoyo.
examples.en: If we cut down on disposables, we can protect the environment.
examples.note: 환경을 보호하다 — the textbook collocation; 줄이다 = to reduce.

examples.ko: 이 회사는 근무 환경이 좋아서 직원들이 오래 다녀요.
examples.romanization: i hoesaneun geunmu hwangyeongi joaseo jigwondeuri orae danyeoyo.
examples.en: This company has a good work environment, so employees stay a long time.
examples.note: Real-situation use of 환경 for workplace conditions, paired with 다니다 (to attend/commute to).

ex.ko: 부모님이 교육이 가장 중요하다고 항상 말씀하세요.
ex.en: My parents always say that education is the most important thing.
ex.note: 중요하다 is an adjective → 중요하다고. 말씀하세요 is the honorific form of 말하다 (말씀하시다), used for parents.

교육.nuance: 교육 is Sino-Korean 敎育 ('teach' 敎 + 'raise/nurture' 育) — literally to teach-and-rear, so it spans schooling, parenting, and on-the-job training, not just classrooms. The crucial direction split is in the verb: the learner says 교육을 받다 ('receive education'), while the provider says 교육하다 or 교육(을) 시키다 ('cause to be educated'). Near-synonym 훈련(訓練) 'training' is narrower and physical/repetitive (군사 훈련 military training, 직업 훈련 vocational training), whereas 교육 includes intellectual and moral formation. In Korea the 공교육(public) vs 사교육(private cram-school) divide is a constant social theme. English-speaker pitfall: don't say 교육을 하다 when you mean 'to study' — that means you're the one teaching; a student always uses 교육을 받다.
교육.explanation: 교육 (gyoyuk) means "education". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 교육을 받다 ("to receive an education"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 교육 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
교육.shortExplanation: 교육 means "education" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 교육을 하다 to mean 'I study/get educated' — 하다 puts you in the teacher's seat; learners use 교육을 받다.
Limiting 교육 to schools — it also covers corporate 교육 (training sessions), parental 교육, and safety briefings (안전 교육).
Using 교육 where 훈련 fits better — repetitive skill drilling (운전 훈련, 군사 훈련) is 훈련, while 교육 is broader teaching.

usagePhrases.note: 받다 (receive) is the learner's-side verb — you take education in.
Add 하다 and it's the teacher's-side verb meaning to teach/train.
공(公) = public; contrasts directly with 사교육 (private tutoring).
Common compound when comparing schools or regions.

examples.en: I want to receive a good education.
examples.note: Simple 교육을 받다 from the learner's side — note 받다, not 하다.

examples.ko: 회사에서 신입 사원을 대상으로 교육을 진행했어요.
examples.romanization: hoesaeseo sinip sawoneul daesangeuro gyoyugeul jinhaenghaesseoyo.
examples.en: The company carried out training for new employees.
examples.note: Everyday workplace sense; -을 대상으로 = targeting, 진행하다 = to conduct.

examples.ko: 한국 부모들은 자녀 교육에 정말 많은 관심을 가져요.
examples.romanization: hanguk bumodeureun janyeo gyoyuge jeongmal maneun gwansimeul gajyeoyo.
examples.en: Korean parents take a great deal of interest in their children's education.
examples.note: Real social topic; 자녀 = one's children (formal), 관심을 가지다 = to take interest.

계시다.en: to be (honorific for 있다 — a person's presence)

ex.en: The boss isn't at his desk right now.
ex.note: 계시다 replaces 있다 when the subject is a person you honor and you are talking about physical presence. 사장님이 있으세요 sounds awkward for the boss's location; 계세요 is the natural respectful form.

계시다.nuance: 계시다 replaces 있다 only for respected people. For things, use 있다: 가방이 있어요, not 가방이 계세요.
계시다.explanation: 계시다 (gyesida) = "to be; to stay (honorific)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 선생님이 교실에 계세요. ("The teacher is in the classroom.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 계시다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
계시다.shortExplanation: 계시다 means "to be; to stay (honorific)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 계시다 for objects or animals without a special respectful reason.
Using 있다 for a respected person in a context where honorifics are expected.

usagePhrases.en: The teacher is in the classroom.
The boss is not here right now.

examples.en: My parents are at home.
examples.note: Respectful way to talk about parents.

드리다.en: to give (humble — you giving to someone senior)

ex.en: I gave my parents a gift.
ex.note: 드리다 is used when YOU give to someone above you. 주다 is the neutral form. 부모님께 uses 께 (honorific 에게).

드리다.nuance: 드리다 respects the recipient, not the subject. It is different from -(으)시-, which honors the subject.
드리다.explanation: 드리다 (deurida) means "to give/do for a respected person (humble)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 부모님께 연락드릴게요. ("I will contact my parents."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 드리다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
드리다.shortExplanation: 드리다 means "to give/do for a respected person (humble)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 제가 오시다 or 제가 드세요 to be polite about yourself. Use 드리다 only when your action goes to someone respected.
Forgetting 께 before the respected recipient.

examples.en: I will guide the customer again.
examples.note: Service-register humble helper.

잡수시다.en: to eat (very honorific for 먹다/드시다 — for very respected elders)

ex.en: Grandma, have you finished your meal?
ex.note: 잡수시다 is higher than 드시다 — reserved for grandparents and very senior people. 진지 is the honorific word for 밥 (meal/rice).

잡수시다.nuance: 드시다 is the safer everyday honorific for eating; 잡수시다 sounds very respectful and elder-focused.
잡수시다.explanation: "to eat (very honorific)" is 잡수시다 (japsusida). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 할머니, 진지 다 잡수셨어요? ("Grandma, have you finished your meal?"). Watch the particle attached to 잡수시다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
잡수시다.shortExplanation: 잡수시다 means "to eat (very honorific)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 잡수시다 for yourself.

usagePhrases.en: Grandma, have you finished your meal?
usagePhrases.note: 진지 is also honorific vocabulary for 밥.

examples.en: Grandfather ate breakfast.
examples.note: 께서 plus 잡수셨어요 marks high respect.

말씀드리다.en: to say / to tell (humble — you speaking to someone senior)

ex.en: I explained my situation to the professor.
ex.note: 말씀드리다 = humble form of 말하다. 교수님께 uses 께 (honorific 에게). Compare: 친구한테 말했어요 (told a friend, plain).

말씀드리다.nuance: 말씀드리다 points upward to the listener. 말씀하시다 is used when the respected person speaks.
말씀드리다.explanation: 말씀드리다 (malsseumdeurida) = "to tell / to say (humble, to someone respected)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 교수님께 사정을 말씀드렸어요. ("I explained the situation to the professor.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 말씀드리다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
말씀드리다.shortExplanation: 말씀드리다 means "to tell / to say (humble, to someone respected)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not say 제가 말씀하셨어요. Use 제가 말씀드렸어요 for your humble action.

usagePhrases.en: I explained the situation to the professor.
usagePhrases.note: This is more natural than 교수님께 말했어요 in a respectful context.

examples.en: I'll tell the team lead that I want to participate.
examples.note: The reported content uses -다고; the speaking verb is humble.

뵙다.en: to meet / to see (humble — you meeting someone senior)

ex.en: Would it be possible to see the professor tomorrow?
ex.note: 뵙다 is the humble form of 만나다/보다 when you are meeting someone you respect. 뵈다 is also used in common conjugations: 뵈어요 → 봬요, 뵈었어요 → 뵀어요.

뵙다.nuance: 뵙다 is humble: it lowers your action of meeting so the other person is respected.
뵙다.explanation: 뵙다 (boepda) means "to meet / to see (humble, someone respected)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 내일 교수님을 뵐 수 있을까요? ("Could I meet the professor tomorrow?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 뵙다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
뵙다.shortExplanation: 뵙다 means "to meet / to see (humble, someone respected)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
For friends, use 만나다 or 보다; 뵙다 is too formal for equal casual relationships.

usagePhrases.en: Could I meet the professor tomorrow?
usagePhrases.note: 뵐 is the future/modifying form of 뵙다.

examples.en: It's nice to meet you for the first time.
examples.note: A fixed formal first-meeting greeting.

발전하다.en: to develop / to advance / to progress

ex.en: The researchers said technology is advancing rapidly.
ex.note: 발전하다 has vowel stem (발전하-) → ㄴ다고: 발전한다고. Classic example of the 다고 pattern with a 하다 verb.

발전하다.nuance: 발전하다 (發展, 'issue-forth + unfold/spread') means to move to a more advanced, mature, or larger stage — technology, economies, skills, companies, even relationships. It is normally intransitive (실력이 발전하다, 경제가 발전하다), and the 'into' target takes ~(으)로 (연인으로 발전하다 = develop into lovers). Its near-synonym 성장하다 ('grow') overlaps but leans biological/scale growth (아이가 성장하다 = a child grows up), whereas 발전하다 stresses qualitative advancement to a higher level. The number-one trap for learners is the look-alike 발견하다 (to discover) — one syllable apart and totally unrelated, so 신약을 발전하다 wrongly means 'develop a new drug' when you meant 발견하다 (discover). The second trap is using 발전하다 transitively; to actively develop something you need the causative 발전시키다 (기술을 발전시켰어요), never 기술을 발전했어요.
발전하다.explanation: "to develop, to advance, to progress" in Korean is 발전하다 (baljeonhada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 발전해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 발전하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 기술이 빠르게 발전하고 있어요. ("Technology is developing fast.") — then reshape the same stem into 발전하고 싶어요 (desire), 발전할 수 있어요 (ability), and 발전할 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
발전하다.shortExplanation: 발전하다 means "to develop, to advance, to progress" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 발전하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 발전해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Don't mix up 발전하다 (develop/advance) with 발견하다 (discover) — one syllable apart, completely different meanings.
To say 'develop X' transitively, use the causative 발전시키다: 기술을 발전시켰어요, not 기술을 발전했어요.
Mark the 'into' goal with ~(으)로, not 을/를: 사업으로 발전했어요 (developed into a business), not 사업을 발전했어요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 발전하다 becomes 발전할 수 있어요 ("can") and 발전할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.en: I develop, to advance, to progress.
I do not develop, to advance, to progress.
I want to develop, to advance, to progress.
I can develop, to advance, to progress.
I have to develop, to advance, to progress.

usagePhrases.note: The thing that develops takes 이/가 — 발전하다 is intransitive (기술이/경제가 발전하다).

examples.en: Our neighborhood has developed a lot.
examples.note: Casual 발전했어 — for places and economies visibly growing over time.

examples.en: If you keep at it, your skills will improve.
examples.note: 실력이 발전하다 = one's skills advance — an encouraging line about steady progress.

examples.en: A small spat escalated into a big fight.
examples.note: Real-situation — 발전하다 can mean a situation escalates ~(으)로 into something bigger, often negative.

ex.en: I think traditions still exist.
ex.note: 생각해요 (I think) also uses the 다고 pattern: 존재한다고 생각해요. 생각하다 is another common reporting verb alongside 하다.
