좋아하다.nuance: 좋아하다 is an action verb meaning 'to like / be fond of', so it describes a person actively having a preference and takes the object marker 을/를: 커피를 좋아해요. Contrast it with the adjective 좋다 ('to be good/nice'), which describes the thing itself and takes 이/가: 커피가 좋아요 ('coffee is nice / I feel good about coffee'). The dividing line is who is in the spotlight — 좋아하다 puts the liker on stage, 좋다 puts the liked thing on stage. Be careful with 사랑하다 ('to love'): Koreans reserve it for deep romantic or familial love and rarely say it about food or hobbies, where English happily uses 'love' — so 'I love coffee' is 커피를 좋아해요, not 커피를 사랑해요. As a 하다 verb it conjugates regularly: 하다 → 해요, giving 좋아해요 / 좋아합니다 / 좋아했어요. The classic English-speaker pitfall is copying English subject logic and saying 커피가 좋아해요 with 이/가; once it is a 좋아하다 sentence, the food must take 을/를.
좋아하다.explanation: 좋아하다 (joahada) = "to like". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 좋아해요 plus one useful sentence like 커피를 좋아해요 ("I like coffee"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 좋아하고 싶어요 for what you want, 좋아할 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 좋아해요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
좋아하다.shortExplanation: 좋아하다 means "to like" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 좋아하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 좋아해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 커피가 좋아해요 with the subject marker — because the verb 좋아하다 needs an object, the food must take 을/를: 커피를 좋아해요.
Using 사랑하다 for liking food or pastimes (커피를 사랑해요) — 사랑하다 sounds like deep romantic/familial love in Korean; for everyday fondness use 좋아하다.
Confusing it with the adjective 좋다 and saying 저는 커피를 좋아요 — if you use the object 를 you must use the verb 좋아해요, not 좋아요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 좋아하다 becomes 좋아할 수 있어요 ("can") and 좋아할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: the thing liked takes the object marker 을/를, not 이/가

examples.en: I like Korean food.
examples.note: the bare polite present states a steady, ongoing preference

examples.en: Our puppy really loves walks.
examples.note: third-person liker takes 이/가 (강아지가), the liked thing still takes 을/를

examples.ko: 저는 매운 음식은 별로 안 좋아해요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun maeun eumsigeun byeollo an joahaeyo.
examples.en: I don't really like spicy food.
examples.note: real refusal: 은 marks the contrast topic, 별로...안 softens the no

ex.en: I dislike coffee that is too sweet.
ex.note: 싫어하다 follows the same object pattern as 좋아하다.

싫어하다.nuance: 싫어하다 is the action verb 'to dislike / hate' and, like its opposite 좋아하다, takes the object marker 을/를: 벌레를 싫어해요. Its adjective partner is 싫다 ('to be unpleasant / not want to'), which takes 이/가 and points at the thing or the feeling itself: 벌레가 싫어요. The verb describes a person's standing dislike, while 싫다 often voices an in-the-moment 'ugh, I don't want to'. The near-synonym to watch is 미워하다, which is 'to resent/hate a person' with an emotional, almost grudge-like color — you 미워하다 someone who hurt you, but you 싫어하다 cold weather or homework. Register matters most here: 싫어해요 is socially strong, so saying 그 사람을 싫어해요 to someone's face is quite blunt; Koreans habitually soften with 별로 ('not really') or simply switch to 별로 안 좋아해요. As a 하다 verb it is regular: 하다 → 해요 (싫어해요 / 싫어합니다 / 싫어했어요). Pitfall: marking the object with 이/가 (벌레가 싫어해요) by mirroring English — keep 을/를 with the verb.
싫어하다.explanation: 싫어하다 (sireohada) means "to dislike". Start from the polite form 싫어해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 싫어하다. A strong first sentence is 벌레를 싫어해요 ("I dislike bugs"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 싫어하다 also becomes 싫어하고 싶어요 (want), 싫어할 수 있어요 (can), and 못 싫어해요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
싫어하다.shortExplanation: 싫어하다 means "to dislike" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 싫어하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 싫어해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Marking the disliked thing with 이/가 (벌레가 싫어해요) — the verb 싫어하다 needs an object, so it must be 벌레를 싫어해요; 이/가 belongs with the adjective 싫다 (벌레가 싫어요).
Using 싫어해요 bluntly about a present person (그 사람을 싫어해요) in front of others — it sounds harsh; soften to 별로 안 좋아해요 or 별로예요.
Reaching for 미워하다 for things like weather or food — 미워하다 is resentment aimed at a person; for objects and situations use 싫어하다.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 싫어하다 becomes 싫어할 수 있어요 ("can") and 싫어할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: the disliked thing takes the object marker 을/를

examples.note: object 를 on the disliked thing; plain steady aversion

ex.ko: 저는 이 카페 커피를 제일 좋아해요.
ex.en: I like this cafe's coffee the most.
ex.note: Use 제일 when choosing the top option.

제일.nuance: 제일 means 'the most / number one' and is the casual, high-frequency spoken twin of 가장. It is Sino-Korean 第一 — literally 'order-one,' i.e. 'first/foremost' — which is why besides modifying adjectives (제일 크다) it can also stand alone like a noun meaning 'the best/top': 건강이 제일이다 = 'health comes first,' 네가 제일이야 = 'you're number one.' 가장 is its near-perfect synonym for the adverb use, the difference being register only: 제일 dominates everyday conversation while 가장 feels a bit more formal/written. Both pick the top of a group of three or more, with the field marked by 중에/에서. The English-speaker pitfall: as with 가장, don't use a superlative for just two items (use 더 instead), and don't glue 제일 onto the noun — 'the cheapest restaurant' is 제일 싼 식당, with 제일 modifying 싼. A further nuance learners miss: because 제일 can be nominal (第一 = 'the first/best'), set expressions like 제일이다 and 제일가다 ('to be foremost') exist, so 그게 제일이야 = 'that's the best option,' not literally 'that is most.' Keep 제일 for talk and texts; switch to 가장 in essays, reports, and formal announcements.
제일.explanation: 제일 (jeil) means "most". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 제일 좋아요. ("It is the best."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 제일 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
제일.shortExplanation: 제일 means "most" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Applying 제일 to only two things; for a two-way comparison use the comparative 더 (둘 중에 이게 더 나아요), and reserve 제일/가장 for three or more.
Putting 제일 directly on the noun; 'the closest station' is 제일 가까운 역, with 제일 modifying the adjective 가까운, not 제일 역.
Treating 제일 as purely adverbial; it can also be nominal (第一), so 건강이 제일이다 = 'health is number one,' which is grammatical and idiomatic.

usagePhrases.note: 제일 + 좋아하다 in a relative clause
Singling out one spot from several
제일 used like a noun: 'the number one'

취향.nuance: 취향 is subjective. 좋아해요 states a preference, while 취향 names the style or taste behind that preference.
취향.explanation: 취향 (chwihyang) means "taste; personal preference". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 제 취향이에요. ("It is my taste."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 취향 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
취향.shortExplanation: 취향 means "taste; personal preference" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 취향 for every objective choice. For price, distance, or time, use comparison expressions instead.
취향 is usually paired with 이/가 or 에: 취향이 달라요, 취향에 맞아요.

usagePhrases.note: A natural way to say something suits your personal preference.
Useful when comparing preferences without arguing.
취향에 맞다 is a very common collocation.

examples.en: Quiet cafes are my taste.
examples.note: Connects preference with a descriptive noun phrase.

examples.en: Our movie tastes are a little different.
examples.note: Common with 영화, 음악, 음식, 옷, and 카페.

ex.en: What is your hobby?
ex.note: A natural topic for 좋아해요 and 비교하다.

취미.nuance: 취미 is Sino-Korean, 趣味 ('interest-taste'), and means a hobby or personal interest. It famously opens small talk: 취미가 뭐예요? — and note it takes 가 there (existence/identity), so a frequent error is ❌취미를 있어요 instead of 취미가 있어요, because 있다 ('to have/exist') is not a transitive verb taking 을/를. To turn an activity into a named hobby, Korean nominalizes the verb with -기: 보다 → 영화 보기 ('movie-watching'), 모으다 → 우표 모으기 ('stamp-collecting'); answering 제 취미는 영화 보기예요 is the model pattern. Distinguish 취미 from 관심: 관심 is broader 'interest/attention' (관심이 있어요 = I'm interested in it), whereas 취미 is specifically a leisure activity you do for fun. The English-speaker pitfall is forcing 있다 into a 'have'-with-object frame (취미를 있어요) — use 취미가 있어요; and don't say ❌취미를 해요 for 'do a hobby' — name the activity itself (영화를 봐요) or say 취미를 즐겨요.
취미.explanation: "hobby" is 취미 (chwimi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 취미가 뭐예요? ("what is your hobby?"). Watch the particle attached to 취미 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
취미.shortExplanation: 취미 means "hobby" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 취미를 있어요 by translating 'have a hobby' as object + have — 있다 takes the subject marker, so 취미가 있어요.
Listing a hobby with a bare verb, e.g. 제 취미는 영화 봐요 — nominalize it: 제 취미는 영화 보기예요.
Confusing 취미 with 관심 — 'I'm interested in K-pop' is 케이팝에 관심이 있어요, whereas 취미 is the leisure activity you actually do.

usagePhrases.note: 있다 'to have/exist' takes the subject marker 가

usagePhrases.en: I started it as a hobby
usagePhrases.note: 취미로 = 'as a hobby', means/role particle 로
topic 는 to name your hobby

examples.en: What is your hobby?
examples.note: the standard ice-breaker; 가, not 를

examples.en: My hobby is watching movies.
examples.note: verb → noun with -기: 보다 → 보기

examples.ko: 취미로 시작한 요리가 이제는 거의 직업이 됐어요.
examples.romanization: chwimiro sijakan yoriga ijeneun geoui jigeobi dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: Cooking, which I started as a hobby, has now almost become a job.

ex.note: Use 차 as a natural comparison partner for coffee.

차.nuance: 차 (茶) is the Sino-Korean word for 'tea,' the brewed leaf or herbal drink, and because it is a beverage it must pair with 마시다 (to drink), never 먹다 (to eat) — though casual speakers do say 차를 먹다 colloquially, learners should default to 마시다. The same syllable 차 (車) also means 'car/vehicle,' so only context separates 차를 마시다 (drink tea) from 차를 타다 (ride a car); they are written identically. Unlike English 'tea,' Korean 차 covers herbal and grain infusions too, so 보리차 (barley tea) and 옥수수차 (corn tea) are 차 even with no tea leaves. A common English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 먹다 by analogy with 'have some tea,' but in standard Korean a polite host says 차 드세요 (드시다 being the honorific of 마시다/먹다). Natural collocations include 차를 우리다 (steep tea) and 차 한 잔 하다 (literally 'do one cup of tea,' meaning to chat over tea).
차.explanation: 차 (cha) means "tea". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 차를 마셔요 ("I drink tea"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 차 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.
차.shortExplanation: 차 means "tea" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 차를 먹어요 in formal contexts: tea is a liquid, so standard Korean uses 마시다 → 차를 마셔요. (먹다 is heard casually but is not the textbook form.)
Confusing 차 'tea' with 차 'car': 차를 타요 means 'I ride a car,' not 'I drink tea.' The verb (마시다 vs 타다) disambiguates the homonym.
Using 을 instead of 를: 차 ends in a vowel, so the object particle is 를 → 차를 마셔요, never 차을 마셔요.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 를 + 마시다 (drink); 차 ends in a vowel so it takes 를, not 을
the verb for letting tea leaves steep; 차를 끓이다 is to boil it
counter 잔 for cups/glasses of liquid; the number 한 (one) comes before the counter

usagePhrases.en: to serve tea to a guest
usagePhrases.note: 대접하다 is a polite, hospitable verb for offering food or drink to someone

examples.en: I drink tea in the morning.
examples.note: Basic habit sentence; 마셔요 is the 요-form of 마시다, which contracts 마시+어요 to 마셔요.

examples.en: Shall I give you a cup of warm tea?
examples.note: 드릴까요 is the humble offering form; note 따뜻한 (warm) modifying the noun directly before 차.

examples.ko: 감기에 걸렸을 때는 따뜻한 유자차를 마시는 게 좋아요.
examples.romanization: gamgie geollyeosseul ttaeneun ttatteutan yujachareul masineun ge joayo.
examples.en: When you catch a cold, it's good to drink warm citron tea.
examples.note: Real-life advice register; 유자차 (citron tea) shows how a flavor word attaches in front of 차.

ex.en: I like exercise as much as my friend does.
ex.note: Useful with 만큼 and 좋아하다.

운동.nuance: 운동 is Sino-Korean, 運動 ('move-motion'), and is the umbrella word for physical exercise; it normally appears as 운동하다 (운동을 해요). Crucially it is NOT counted or pluralized like English 'a workout' — you don't say 운동들 for several sessions; you say 운동을 자주 해요. The nearest relative is 스포츠 (a borrowed word for organized sports as a category, e.g. watching 스포츠 on TV), whereas 운동 is the act of exercising your own body, so '운동선수' = athlete but '스포츠 경기' = a sports match. The very same 運動 also means a social 'movement/campaign' (민주화 운동 the democracy movement), so context decides. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 만들다 ('make') by analogy with 'make exercise' — Korean uses the light verb 하다; and remember the desire ending goes on the verb (운동하고 싶어요), never on the bare noun.
운동.explanation: 운동 (undong) means "exercise". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 운동을 해요 ("I exercise"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 운동 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
운동.shortExplanation: 운동 means "exercise" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 운동을 만들어요 by translating 'do/make exercise' literally — 만들다 means physically craft something; the correct light verb is 하다, so 운동을 해요.
Attaching the want-ending to the noun as 운동 싶어요 — -고 싶다 only fastens to a verb stem, so it must be 운동하고 싶어요 / 운동을 하고 싶어요.
Using 운동들 to mean several workouts — 운동 is non-count here; say 운동을 여러 번 해요 or 자주 운동해요 instead.

usagePhrases.note: 운동 takes the object marker 을 because 하다 acts on it
subject marker 이 after a consonant
-고 싶어요 attaches to the verb 하-, not to the noun
좋아하다 is a verb 'to like', so its object takes 을/를

examples.en: I exercise every day.
examples.note: the everyday 운동하다 frame for a habit

examples.en: I started exercising lately to lose weight.
examples.note: 운동을 시작하다 = take up working out

examples.ko: 헬스장에서 한 시간 동안 운동했더니 온몸이 뻐근해요.
examples.romanization: helseujangeseo han sigan dongan undonghaetdeoni onmomi ppeogeunhaeyo.
examples.en: After working out at the gym for an hour, my whole body is stiff.
examples.note: real gym talk; 운동하다 contracted, with a result

ex.en: Let's compare the price and our preferences.
ex.note: Use 비교하다 for deliberate comparison.

비교하다.nuance: 비교하다 is the Sino-Korean verb 比較(비교, 'compare-contrast') + 하다, meaning to set two or more things side by side to weigh their differences. The thing(s) compared take 을/를, and the second item of a pair takes 와/과 (formal) or 하고/랑 (casual): A를 B와 비교하다. Being a 하다 verb it conjugates to 해요 (never 하요) and 했어요. Distinguish it from 대조하다 (對照, 'contrast'), which highlights opposites for academic effect, while 비교하다 is the neutral everyday word ('compare prices, compare two phones'). The big English-speaker pitfall is the particle: learners copy English 'compare A to B' and say 가격에 비교해요, but the object marker must be 을/를 — 가격을 비교해요. Note too the social weight of 비교당하다 ('to be compared', passive): Koreans dislike being measured against others, so 비교하지 마 ('stop comparing me') is emotionally loaded.
비교하다.explanation: 비교하다 (bigyohada) means "to compare". Start from the polite form 비교해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 비교하다. A strong first sentence is 가격을 비교하다 ("to compare prices"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 비교하다 also becomes 비교하고 싶어요 (want), 비교할 수 있어요 (can), and 비교할 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
비교하다.shortExplanation: 비교하다 means "to compare" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 비교하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 비교해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 가격에 비교해요 with 에, copied from English 'compare to'. The thing compared is a direct object, so it must take 을/를: 가격을 비교해요.
Writing the present tense as 비교하요. Every 하다 verb contracts 하 + 여 to 해, so the form is 비교해요 / 비교했어요, never 비교하요.
Marking the second item of a pair with 을/를 too (이것을 저것을 비교해요). The compared-against partner takes 와/과: 이것을 저것과 비교해요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 비교하다 becomes 비교할 수 있어요 ("can") and 비교할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: The single most common collocation; Koreans 가격 비교 ('price comparison') before any purchase.

examples.en: I compare prices
examples.note: The plainest frame: object + 을/를 + 비교해요, an everyday shopping habit.

examples.ko: 사기 전에 두 제품을 비교해 봤어요
examples.romanization: sagi jeone du jepumeul bigyohae bwasseoyo
examples.en: Before buying, I compared the two products
examples.note: 사기 전에 ('before buying') + 비교해 봤어요 ('tried comparing') is exactly how a shopper talks.

examples.en: Please don't compare (your child) with others' children
examples.note: 남(의) ('other people's') + 와 + 비교하지 마세요 — a heartfelt request, the social side of this verb.

ex.en: I chose coffee.
ex.note: A practical verb after comparing options.

선택하다.nuance: 선택하다 is 選擇(선택, 'select-pick') + 하다 and means to pick a defined option from a presented set — menus, app settings, multiple-choice answers, life paths. It is the bookish, neutral register; in spoken everyday Korean the native verb 고르다 ('pick out') is warmer and more common ('과일을 골랐어요'). Crucially, contrast it with 결정하다 (決定, 'decide'): 선택하다 is choosing one option among several that already exist, while 결정하다 is settling a matter or reaching a conclusion ('유학을 결정했어요' = decided to study abroad). As a 하다 verb it gives 선택해요 / 선택했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle and the 고르다 split: say 메뉴를 선택해요 with 을/를 (not 메뉴에), and don't force 선택하다 into casual chat where a native would simply say 골라요. Also, 'choose to do X' is not 선택하다 alone — Korean prefers ~기로 하다/결심하다.
선택하다.explanation: "to choose" in Korean is 선택하다 (seontaekhada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 선택해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 선택하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 하나를 선택하다 ("to choose one (item)") — then reshape the same stem into 선택하고 싶어요 (desire), 선택할 수 있어요 (ability), and 선택할 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
선택하다.shortExplanation: 선택하다 means "to choose" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 선택하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 선택해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 선택하다 to translate every English 'choose', including 'I chose to stay'. For 'choose to do', Korean uses ~기로 하다: 남기로 했어요, not 남는 것을 선택했어요.
Marking the option with 에 (메뉴에 선택해요) under the influence of English. The chosen thing is a direct object: 메뉴를 선택해요.
Treating 선택하다 and 결정하다 as interchangeable. 선택하다 = pick an existing option; 결정하다 = decide/settle a matter. 'I decided' is 결정했어요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 선택하다 becomes 선택할 수 있어요 ("can") and 선택할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: Object + 을/를 + 선택하다; 하나만 선택하세요 ('pick only one') is standard quiz/form wording.

examples.en: I chose the blue one
examples.note: Plain object frame: color + 을/를 + 선택했어요, e.g. picking a phone case.

examples.en: Please select your menu on the kiosk
examples.note: 에서 ('at/on') the kiosk + 선택해 주세요 — exactly what a café screen tells you.

examples.ko: 둘 다 좋아서 하나를 선택하기 어려워요
examples.romanization: dul da joaseo hanareul seontaekagi eoryeowoyo
examples.en: Both are good, so it's hard to pick one
examples.note: 선택하기 어렵다 ('hard to choose') turns the verb into a noun with -기.

ex.en: Going by subway is fast.
ex.note: Use 지하철로 for 'by subway' and 지하철을 타요 for boarding.

지하철.nuance: 지하철 is the subway system; 지하철역 is the subway station.
지하철.explanation: "subway" is 지하철 (jihacheol). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 지하철을 타요 ("I take the subway."). Watch the particle attached to 지하철 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off first, then vary one word.
지하철.shortExplanation: 지하철 means "subway" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Use 지하철을 타요 for taking it; use 지하철로 가요 for going by subway.

examples.en: I take the subway.
examples.note: Transportation.

examples.en: Can I go by subway?
examples.note: Method.

examples.en: Where is the subway station?
examples.note: Question.

ex.en: The bus broke down, so I ended up late.
ex.note: A transport noun that naturally pairs with 바람에.

버스.nuance: 버스 is useful with 타다, 기다리다, 내리다, and 로/으로 for transportation method.
버스.explanation: 버스 (beoseu) = "bus". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 버스를 타요 ("I take the bus.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 버스, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.
버스.shortExplanation: 버스 means "bus" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not say 버스에 타요 as your first pattern; 버스를 타요 is the beginner frame.

examples.en: I take the bus.
examples.note: Transportation.

examples.en: I wait for the bus.
examples.note: Waiting.

examples.en: I get off at the next stop.
examples.note: Travel.

ex.en: Because of the rain, I could not take a taxi.
ex.note: Keeps 때문에 attached to a real noun.

택시.nuance: 택시로 가요 and 택시를 타요 are both natural, but they answer different questions: method versus boarding action.
택시.explanation: 택시 (taeksi) = "taxi". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 택시를 타다 ("to take a taxi") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 택시, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
택시.shortExplanation: 택시 means "taxi" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 택시에 가요 for 'by taxi.' Use 택시로 가요.
Forgetting 을/를 in 택시를 타요 when the focus is taking the vehicle.
Using 택시로 타요; 타다 takes the vehicle as object, not method.

usagePhrases.note: The vehicle you board takes 을/를.

examples.en: If you do not have time, go by taxi.
examples.note: 택시로 marks the means of travel.

examples.en: It rained, so I took a taxi.
examples.note: 택시를 타다 is the boarding/taking frame.

examples.en: Please call me a taxi.
examples.note: A practical request at hotels, restaurants, and stations.

ex.en: Transfer to Line 2 at the station.
ex.note: The station where an action happens takes 에서.

역.nuance: 역 (驛, 'relay station / post-horse stage') means a train or subway station and almost always attaches to a place or line name — 서울역, 강남역, 부산역. It is the everyday navigation anchor of Korean city life, with people meeting and giving directions by 출구 (exit) number. Distinguish it from 정류장 (停留場), which is a *bus stop* — buses stop at a 버스 정류장, not a 역, so don't mix them. The historical hanja 驛 refers to old relay-horse posts, now repurposed for rail. Beware two look-alikes: 역할 (役割, 'role') and the particle/adverb 역시 ('as expected') share the syllable 역 but are unrelated words. The reliable English-speaker error is particles: 역에 가요 for going to the station (에 = destination) but 역에서 만나요 / 기차를 타요 for an action at the station (에서); never say 역에서 가요 when you mean 'go there'.
역.explanation: 역 (yeok) means "station". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 지하철역 ("a subway station"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 역 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.
역.shortExplanation: 역 means "station" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a bus stop a 역. Trains and subways stop at a 역, but buses stop at a 정류장 (버스 정류장). 'I'll wait at the bus stop' = 버스 정류장에서 기다릴게요, not 역에서.
Saying 역에서 가요 for 'I go to the station'. Going there takes 에 (역에 가요); 에서 is for an action done at the station, e.g. 역에서 만나요.
Confusing 역(驛, station) with 역할(役割, role). They share one syllable but are different words: 강남역 = Gangnam Station, but 역할이 중요해요 = 'the role is important'.

usagePhrases.note: 지하철 'subway' + 역; the most common compound, since urban Koreans live by subway lines.
에 marks the destination with 가다/오다.
에서 = where the meeting happens; stations are the default Korean meeting point.
출구 (出口) = exit; Koreans navigate by exit number — '3번 출구에서 만나' ('meet at exit 3').

examples.en: The station is close.
examples.note: Simple description; 가깝다 'to be near'. A big plus when renting a room.

examples.en: I took the train at Seoul Station.
examples.note: 서울역 = Seoul Station; 에서 because boarding happens at the station; 타다 'to ride/board'.

examples.en: I'll come out of exit 3 and wait in front of the station.
examples.note: ~(으)로 나오다 'come out via'; 앞에서 'in front of' + 에서 marks the waiting spot.

ex.en: I go to the bus stop to take the bus.
ex.note: 정류장에 is the destination; 타러 is the purpose.

정류장.nuance: 정류장 is the stop itself. 역 is a station, usually larger and often for subway or train.
정류장.explanation: 정류장 (jeongnyujang) means "bus stop; stop". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 버스 정류장 ("bus stop"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 정류장 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
정류장.shortExplanation: 정류장 means "bus stop; stop" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 역 for every bus stop. For buses, 정류장 is normally better.
Saying 정류장으로 내려요. Use 정류장에서 내려요 because getting off happens at the stop.
Forgetting the destination/action split: 정류장에 가요, 정류장에서 기다려요.

usagePhrases.en: to get off at the stop
usagePhrases.note: The place where the action happens takes 에서.

examples.en: I go to the bus stop to take the bus.
examples.note: 타러 gives purpose; 정류장에 gives destination.

examples.en: Get off at the next stop.
examples.note: 내리다 happens at the stop, so 에서.

examples.en: Where is the bus stop?
examples.note: Useful direction question.

ex.en: Keep going straight on this road.
ex.note: Often used in directions with 길로.

직진.nuance: 직진 is Sino-Korean, 直進, literally 'straight-advance' (直 straight + 進 to go forward) — proceeding straight ahead without turning, the third member of the navigation trio with 우회전 and 좌회전. Spoken GPS commands chain them: 직진하다가 좌회전 ('go straight, then turn left'). Its everyday spoken cousins on foot are 쭉 가세요 or 똑바로 가세요 ('go straight on'), so like its turn-siblings, 직진 itself leans toward driving and GPS speech; saying 직진하세요 to someone walking sounds a little mechanical. It pairs with 하다 (직진하다), 계속, 신호, 차선. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb: 직진 is a noun, so 'go straight' is 직진하다, not 직진 가다 — and don't substitute the bare verb 가다 for it. Also, a 직진 차선 (through lane) legally forbids turning, a nuance the plain English 'straight' doesn't carry, so read lane markings before assuming you can turn.
직진.explanation: "going straight ahead" is 직진 (jikjin). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 직진하다 ("to go straight"). Watch the particle attached to 직진 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.
직진.shortExplanation: 직진 means "going straight ahead" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Pairing 직진 with the wrong verb — it takes 하다 (직진하다), not 직진 가다; 직진 is a noun and needs 하다 to become an action
Using 직진 for walking when 쭉 가세요 or 똑바로 가세요 is more natural — 직진 sounds like a driving/GPS command
Assuming you can still turn from a 직진 차선 — a 'through lane' legally allows only going straight, so you must change lanes earlier to turn

usagePhrases.note: add 하다 to make the verb

examples.en: Keep going straight.
examples.note: 계속 = continuously; the single most common GPS instruction

examples.en: Go straight, then turn right.
examples.note: 다가 = and then switch mid-action; chains 직진 with a turn the way navigation does

examples.ko: 이 차선은 직진만 돼서 여기서 좌회전 못 해요.
examples.romanization: i chaseoneun jikjinman dwaeseo yeogiseo jwahoejeon mo taeyo.
examples.en: This lane is straight-only, so you can't turn left here.
examples.note: 만 = only; real driving constraint, 직진 차선 forbids turning

ex.en: I transfer at City Hall Station.
ex.note: Official transit word; 갈아타다 is the everyday verb.

환승.nuance: 환승 means transferring between buses and subways. If you tap the same transit card, transfers within a time limit are usually discounted or free.
환승.explanation: 환승 (hwanseung) = "transfer (transit)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 어디서 환승해요? ("Where do I transfer?") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 환승, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.
환승.shortExplanation: 환승 means "transfer (transit)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Tap your card when getting off too, or you may lose the 환승 transfer discount.

examples.en: I transfer at City Hall Station.
examples.note: Place.

examples.en: I transferred from bus to subway.
examples.note: Route.

examples.en: It is cheaper if you transfer with one card.
examples.note: Condition.

ex.en: Transfer to Line 2.
ex.note: The line or vehicle you transfer into takes 으로/로.

갈아타다.nuance: 갈아타다 is a transparent compound of 갈다 'to change/replace' + 타다 'to ride', so it literally means 'change-ride' — you get off one vehicle and board a different one. The dividing line learners must feel is against plain 타다 (just 'to board/get on') and against 환승하다, the Sino-Korean twin (換乘, 換 'exchange' + 乘 'ride', literally 'change-ride') printed on every subway sign and announcement: 갈아타다 is the warm spoken word a friend uses ('여기서 갈아타'), while 환승하다 is the signage/official register ('환승 게이트'). The grammar trap is the particle: the vehicle you move TO takes 로/으로 (지하철로 갈아타다), the same directional 로 as 'change INTO', and the station where you do it takes 에서 — English 'transfer to the subway' tempts you to drop the particle or use 에. Because 타다 is regular, every form is regular too: the stem 타- already ends in ㅏ, so the 아 of 아요 merges in and disappears, giving 갈아타요 (not 갈아타아요), and the past is 갈아탔어요. Habitual collocations: 다른 노선으로 갈아타다, 같은 방향으로 갈아타다.
갈아타다.explanation: 갈아타다 (garata-da) = "to transfer". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 갈아타요 plus one useful sentence like 지하철로 갈아타다 ("to transfer to the subway"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 갈아타고 싶어요 for what you want, 갈아탈 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 갈아타요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off.
갈아타다.shortExplanation: 갈아타다 means "to transfer" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 갈아타다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 갈아타요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 지하철에 갈아타요 with 에. The destination vehicle is the thing you change INTO, so it needs directional 로/으로: 지하철로 갈아타요.
Using 타다 when you mean 'transfer': 버스를 타요 only means 'I board a bus', not 'I switch from another vehicle to the bus'. To express the switch you must use 갈아타다: 버스로 갈아타요.
Writing the polite form as 갈아타아요. 타다 already ends in ㅏ, so the 아 of 아요 merges and disappears — the correct form is 갈아타요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 갈아타다 becomes 갈아탈 수 있어요 ("can") and 갈아탈 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

타다.nuance: Use 타다 for getting on or riding transportation: 버스를 타요, 지하철을 타요.
타다.explanation: 타다 (tada) means "to ride / take". Start from the polite form 타요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 타다. A strong first sentence is 버스를 타요 ("take the bus."); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 타다 also becomes 타고 싶어요 (want), 탈 수 있어요 (can), and 못 타요 (cannot). 길.nuance: 길 can mean road, path, way, or route. 길을 잃었어요 is a survival phrase.
길.explanation: 길 (gil) means "road / way". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 길을 찾아요 ("I look for the way."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 길 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. 방향.nuance: 방향 is Sino-Korean 方向 (方 'direction/region' + 向 'to face/head toward'), the abstract heading or orientation of movement. The central contrast is 방향 vs 쪽: 쪽 is the concrete, point-at-it 'side/way' right in front of you (이쪽, 저쪽, 오른쪽), while 방향 is the abstract course of travel you reason about — 'the opposite direction', 'the right direction', 'which way leads there'. So you point 이쪽 ('this way, here') but you verify 방향이 맞아요? ('am I heading right?') and warn 반대 방향이에요 ('that's the wrong way'). Compare 위치 too: 위치 is where something is (static position), 방향 is which way it faces or you move. Register neutral, fine in speech and signs (e.g., 부산 방향 on a road sign = 'toward Busan'). English-speaker pitfalls: for movement use 으로 (반대 방향으로 가요), not 에 (방향에 가요 is wrong); and don't confuse 방향 with the look-alike 방학 (school vacation) — same 방, unrelated meanings.
방향.explanation: 방향 (banghyang) = "direction". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 방향이 맞다 ("the direction is right") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 방향, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.
방향.shortExplanation: 방향 means "direction" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Using 방향 where 쪽 fits better. To point at a concrete side say 이쪽/저쪽; 방향 is the abstract course of travel.

부탁하다.nuance: 부탁하다 is 付託(부탁)하다, hanja 付 'hand over' + 託 'entrust', so the image is entrusting a task into someone's hands — you are asking them to do something FOR you, leaning on their goodwill. Contrast it sharply with 요청하다 and 시키다: 부탁하다 is personal and humble (you owe a thank-you), 요청하다 is formal/institutional (자료를 요청하다 'request documents'), and 시키다 is to MAKE/order someone do it from a position of authority — never use 시키다 with someone older or you sound bossy. The famous phrase 잘 부탁합니다 has no clean English equivalent; it pre-thanks someone for the cooperation you're about to receive and is near-mandatory in introductions. English speakers misfire two ways: they try to use 부탁하다 to order food or goods (that is 주문하다), and they attach the favor with the wrong particle — the person is 에게/한테, and the favor itself, if stated, is the object: 친구에게 부탁을 했어요. As a 하다 verb it is fully regular, negating as 부탁 안 해요.
부탁하다.explanation: "to ask a favor" in Korean is 부탁하다 (butakada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 부탁해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 부탁하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 잘 부탁합니다 ("I'm counting on you / nice to work with you") — then reshape the same stem into 부탁하고 싶어요 (desire), 부탁할 수 있어요 (ability), and 부탁 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. Swapping in 시키다 to be polite. 시키다 means to order/make someone do it and sounds bossy to elders; humble requests use 부탁하다.

usagePhrases.en: I do not ask a favor.
I want to ask a favor.
I have to ask a favor.
I'm counting on you / nice to work with you
usagePhrases.note: The single most-used set phrase — said when starting a job, a class, or any relationship

examples.en: Take care of this for me, please.
examples.note: Simple: 좀 softens the ask between friends — banmal 부탁해 is casual but warm

examples.en: I was busy, so I asked my sibling to do the dishes.
examples.note: Everyday: the task (설거지를) + the person (동생에게) both appear

examples.ko: 부탁이 하나 있는데, 들어주실 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: butagi hana inneunde, deureojusil su isseoyo?
examples.en: I have a favor to ask — could you grant it?
examples.note: Real situation: the polite framing 부탁이 있는데 sets up a request before stating it

ex.en: Should I try on these clothes?
ex.note: Core noun for trying on clothing.

옷.nuance: 옷 is a pure native Korean word (no hanja) meaning clothes/clothing for the body, and the verb you MUST pair it with is 입다 (to wear on the torso/body) — never 신다, which is reserved for footwear on the feet (신발을 신다), nor 쓰다 (hats/glasses) nor 끼다 (gloves/rings). English 'wear/put on' covers every garment with one verb, so this split is the central pitfall: 옷을 신어요 is a classic beginner error. To take clothes off is 벗다, to change them 갈아입다. For 'these clothes look good on you,' Korean says 옷이 잘 어울려요 (the clothes suit you), not a direct translation of 'you look good.' Note 옷 is treated as singular/uncountable grammatically (no plural needed): one outfit or a wardrobe full is still just 옷. The dressier counterpart 의상 (costume/attire, 衣裳) is for performances or formal contexts. Register is neutral and everyday.
옷.explanation: 옷 (ot) means "clothes". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 옷을 입다 ("to put on/wear clothes"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 옷 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.
옷.shortExplanation: 옷 means "clothes" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 옷을 신어요 to mean 'I wear clothes.' 신다 is only for footwear; clothing on the body takes 옷을 입어요.
Forcing a plural like 옷들을 입어요 for several garments. 옷 is uncountable here — 옷을 입어요 already covers any amount.
Translating 'you look good in that' word-for-word. Korean idiom is 그 옷이 잘 어울려요 (the clothes suit you), using 어울리다, not a literal 'you look good.'

usagePhrases.note: 입다 is the body-clothing verb; object 을
pair verb to 입다 for the torso/body
어울리다 collocation for looking good on you

examples.en: What should I wear today?
examples.note: 입다 + -ㄹ까요 (shall I/what shall); 옷 is implied, not stated

examples.en: I sweated so I changed my clothes.
examples.note: 갈아입다 → 갈아입었어요; -아서 gives the reason

examples.ko: 그 옷이 너한테 정말 잘 어울려.
examples.romanization: geu osi neohante jeongmal jal eoullyeo.
examples.en: Those clothes really suit you.
examples.note: 반말; 어울리다 = suit/look good on; 한테 = on/to you

ex.en: Please recommend another color too.
ex.note: Useful in clothing and shopping suggestions.

색.nuance: 색 is the Sino-Korean root 色 ('color'), and it appears both as a standalone noun and, more often in casual speech, expanded to 색깔 — the two are interchangeable, with 색깔 feeling slightly warmer and more spoken. As a suffix, 색 attaches to color stems to make full color nouns: 빨간색, 파란색, 노란색. There is also a fixed set of bare Sino-Korean color words — 녹색(綠色) green, 황색(黃色) yellow, 흑색(黑色) black — used in formal or technical registers. The English-speaker pitfall is the object particle: 좋아하다 ('to like') takes a direct object, so 'I like this color' must be 이 색을 좋아해요, with 을, even though English 'like' feels stative. Note too that 좋아하다 expresses a held preference, whereas 마음에 들다 ('it pleases me') is for a fresh, in-the-moment liking of one specific thing.
색.explanation: 색 (saek) means "color". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 무슨 색이에요? ("what color is it?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 색 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
색.shortExplanation: 색 means "color" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Dropping the object particle and saying 밝은 색 좋아해요; 좋아하다 needs an object, so the natural form is 밝은 색을 좋아해요.
Using 좋아하다 to react to one item you just saw; for an on-the-spot 'I like this one' Koreans prefer 이 색이 마음에 들어요.
Treating 색깔 as more formal than 색; it is actually the more casual, conversational form, while bare 색 and Sino words like 녹색 lean formal.

examples.en: What color is this bag?
examples.note: asking someone's color

examples.en: I like bright colors.
examples.note: object 을 + 좋아하다

examples.en: I really like this color.
examples.note: 마음에 들다 = to be to one's taste

어울리다.en: to suit; to look good on

ex.en: This color suits you well.
ex.note: Use the 'to suit' sense, not the 'hang out' sense.

어울리다.nuance: 어울리다 carries two everyday meanings bound by one idea — 'to harmonize / fit together well': (1) to suit or look good on someone (이 옷이 잘 어울려요 = this suits you), and (2) to mingle, blend in, or get along with people (친구들하고 잘 어울려요). The particle pattern is the crux for English speakers, because English 'suits you' makes 'you' the object: in Korean the thing that suits is the SUBJECT and takes 이/가 (옷이 어울려요, never 옷을 어울려요), the person it suits is unmarked or takes 한테/에게, and a matching partner or group takes 하고/와/과 (치마하고 어울리다, 사람들하고 어울리다); a setting it fits takes 에 (분위기에 어울리다). Conjugation is the regular ㅣ-vowel contraction, not an irregular: 어울리 + 어 fuses to 어울려, giving polite 어울려요 and past 어울렸어요 (not 어울리어요). A useful contrast: 어울리다 ('look good / harmonize') vs 맞다 ('fit in size / be correct') — clothes that 어울리다 flatter you, clothes that 맞다 are the right size, and the two are not the same compliment.
어울리다.explanation: 어울리다 (eoullida) means "to suit". Start from the polite form 어울려요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 어울리다. A strong first sentence is 이 옷이 잘 어울려요 ("This outfit suits (you) well"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 어울리다 also becomes 어울리고 싶어요 (want), 어울릴 수 있어요 (can), and 어울릴 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
어울리다.shortExplanation: 어울리다 means "to suit" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 어울리다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 어울려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 을/를 for what suits you — say 옷이 어울려요 (이/가), never 옷을 어울려요; the flattering thing is the subject.
Writing 어울리어요 instead of the contracted 어울려요 — the stem-final ㅣ fuses with 어 to 려.
Confusing 어울리다 (look good / harmonize) with 맞다 (fit in size / be correct) — 'this suits you' is 어울려요, 'this fits (size)' is 맞아요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 어울리다 becomes 어울릴 수 있어요 ("can") and 어울릴 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: What looks good on you takes 이/가, not 을/를 — 옷이 어울려요, paired with 잘 ('well').

examples.en: That color really suits you
examples.note: A natural compliment; note 색이 (이/가), since the color is what suits.

examples.en: These shoes go well with the skirt
examples.note: Item + 하고 어울리다 = two things match each other.

examples.en: I quickly mixed in with the new coworkers
examples.note: Past 어울렸어요 in the 'get along / fit in' sense, with 금방 ('quickly').

ex.en: If the size is big, please exchange it.
ex.note: 바꿔 주세요 is a practical service request.

바꾸다.nuance: 바꾸다 means to replace one thing with another, or to alter something into a different state — money (돈을 바꾸다), seats (자리를 바꾸다), plans (계획을 바꾸다), even your mind (마음을 바꾸다). The dividing line from 고치다 is essential: 바꾸다 ends with a DIFFERENT thing, 고치다 keeps the SAME thing repaired. Returning a defective shirt for a new one is 옷을 바꾸다; mending the torn seam is 옷을 고치다. The destination of the change takes the particle -(으)로: 작은 걸로 바꿔 주세요 ('change it for the small one'). Note also 바뀌다, the intransitive twin: 바꾸다 is 'I change X' (transitive, takes 을/를), while 바뀌다 is 'X changes by itself' (신호등이 바뀌었어요 = 'the light changed') — mixing these up is a frequent error. Conjugation is regular: 바꾸 + 어요 → 바꿔요, past 바꿨어요. English-speaker pitfall: 'change my mind' is 마음을 바꾸다, not 생각을 고치다, and 'change clothes (get dressed)' is 옷을 갈아입다, not 옷을 바꾸다.
바꾸다.explanation: 바꾸다 (bakkuda) means "to change". Start from the polite form 바꿔요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 바꾸다. A strong first sentence is 돈을 바꾸다 ("to exchange money"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 바꾸다 also becomes 바꾸고 싶어요 (want), 바꿀 수 있어요 (can), and 못 바꿔요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
바꾸다.shortExplanation: 바꾸다 means "to change" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 바꾸다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 바꿔요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 바꾸다 for repairing — fixing the same broken item is 고치다; 바꾸다 means swapping it for a different one.
Confusing 바꾸다 with 바뀌다 — 바꾸다 needs an object (제가 약속을 바꿨어요), but 'it changed on its own' is 바뀌었어요 with no object.
Saying 옷을 바꾸다 for 'change clothes/get changed' — that's 옷을 갈아입다; 옷을 바꾸다 means exchange the garment at a store.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 바꾸다 becomes 바꿀 수 있어요 ("can") and 바꿀 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: for currency exchange Koreans say 돈을 바꾸다 / 환전하다; 달러로 바꿔요 ('change into dollars')

examples.en: I change my name.
examples.note: Simple object + verb; stem 바꾸 + 어요 → 바꿔요 (ㅜ+어 contracts to 워)

examples.en: The size didn't fit, so I exchanged the clothes.
examples.note: -아서 gives the reason; the target size would take -(으)로

examples.en: Could you switch seats with me?
examples.note: Real request on a train/plane; 바꿔 주세요 asks the other person to do the swap

ex.ko: 한 치수 작은 것도 보여 주세요.
ex.en: Please show me one size smaller too.
ex.note: 보여 주세요 is the request form used in shops.

보이다.nuance: 보이다 is the passive/spontaneous counterpart of 보다 (to look): something enters your field of vision on its own, so the thing seen takes 이/가 (산이 보여요 = 'the mountain is visible'), NOT 을/를. The 요-form contracts 보이-+-어요 → 보여요 (past 보였어요). The sharp contrast learners need is 보이다 vs 보다: 보다 is an active choice ('I look at / watch'), 보이다 is involuntary ('it is seen / comes into view'). A second, very frequent meaning is 'to look/seem' — adjective stem + 보이다 (행복해 보여요 'you look happy'; 비싸 보여요 'it looks expensive'); here English 'looks' maps cleanly. With 주다 it flips to active 'show' (보여 주다). The English-speaker pitfall: saying 산을 보여요 to mean 'I see the mountain' — that is wrong; use 산이 보여요 (it is visible) or 산을 봐요 (I look at it).
보이다.explanation: 보이다 (boi-da) means "to be seen". Start from the polite form 보여요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 보이다. A strong first sentence is 잘 보이다 ("to be clearly visible"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 보이다 also becomes 보이고 싶어요 (want), 보일 수 있어요 (can), and 못 보여요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
보이다.shortExplanation: 보이다 means "to be seen" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 보이다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 보여요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Marking the seen thing with 을/를: 글씨를 안 보여요 is wrong. Because 보이다 is intransitive, say 글씨가 안 보여요 ('the letters aren't visible').
Confusing 보이다 with 보다. 'I can see it' for involuntary vision is 보여요, but 'I look at it / watch it' is 봐요 — don't use 보여요 for deliberate watching.
Forgetting the 'looks like' meaning. 'You look tired' is 피곤해 보여요, not 피곤한 것을 봐요 — adjective stem + 보이다 carries the 'seems' sense.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 보이다 becomes 보일 수 있어요 ("can") and 보일 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: 잘 (well) is the habitual partner for visibility; opposite is 안 보이다.

examples.en: The sea is very visible from here.
examples.note: The thing seen takes 이/가 (바다가), not 을/를 — this is intransitive.

examples.en: Please show me your ticket.
examples.note: 보여 주다 = 'show'; here it IS transitive because of 주다, so 표를 takes 를.

examples.en: You look tired. Get some rest.
examples.note: Adjective stem 피곤하- + 보여요 = 'looks ~', a hugely common everyday use.

ex.en: It is good. But it is a little expensive.
ex.note: A softer pivot than 하지만.

그런데.nuance: 그런데 (spoken: 근데) is the soft, all-purpose 'but' that also works as 'by the way' to glide into a new topic — this double life surprises English speakers most. As contrast it is far gentler than 하지만 or 그렇지만; it doesn't slam two ideas together, it just notes that something slightly different follows. As a topic-changer it carries no contrast at all: 그런데, 우리 언제 만나요? simply means 'So/Anyway, when shall we meet?'. It is closely tied to the mid-sentence ending -는데, which sets background before a turn (비싼데 살까? = it's pricey, but shall I buy it?). The everyday pitfall is over-translating it as a strong 'however'; if you mean a firm, contrastive 'however', reach for 하지만. And don't write the long form in chat — Koreans type 근데.
그런데.explanation: "but; by the way" is 그런데 (geureonde). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 그런데 ("but / by the way"). Watch the particle attached to 그런데 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
그런데.shortExplanation: 그런데 means "but; by the way" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 그런데 always means 'but'. Very often it just means 'by the way / so' and introduces zero contrast, as in 그런데 이거 얼마예요? (By the way, how much is this?).
Using 그런데 where you need a strong, clear 'however'. For a firm contrast 하지만/그렇지만 is stronger; 그런데 stays soft.
Saying 그런데 in fast casual speech. It's not wrong, but it sounds bookish — natural spoken Korean contracts it to 근데.

usagePhrases.note: Soft contrast OR a gentle pivot to a new topic.

usagePhrases.en: It's nice. But it's a bit pricey.
usagePhrases.note: Mild 'but' that softens the bad news.

usagePhrases.en: by the way, here's the thing…
usagePhrases.note: Set phrase that eases you into a new subject.
In speech almost everyone shortens it to 근데.

examples.ko: 이 식당 맛있어요. 그런데 사람이 너무 많아요.
examples.romanization: i sikdang masisseoyo. geureonde sarami neomu manayo.
examples.en: This place is tasty. But there are way too many people.
examples.note: Two facts, gently set against each other.

examples.ko: 잘 지냈어요? 그런데 그 얘기 들었어요?
examples.romanization: jal jinaesseoyo? geureonde geu yaegi deureosseoyo?
examples.en: Have you been well? By the way, did you hear that news?
examples.note: Here it isn't 'but' at all — it just changes the subject.

examples.en: I'd like to order — but is this spicy?
examples.note: Real ordering moment; softens straight into a question.

cluster.title: 그리고 vs 그래서 vs 그런데 vs 그러면
cluster.rule: Pick by the logical link back to the sentence you just said: 그리고 simply adds, 그래서 gives its result, 그런데 turns away from it, and 그러면 treats it as a premise ("if that's so, then…"). Note that in real speech 그런데/근데 is very often not contrast at all — it's just "by the way", a way to slide into a new topic.

example.en: I had dinner. And then I drank coffee.
It's raining. So I'm staying home.

members.when: soft contrast, or changing the topic

example.en: By the way, when are we meeting?

members.en: then, in that case, if so
members.when: reacting to what was just said

ex.en: It is delicious. However, it is expensive.
ex.note: Use at the start of a new sentence.

하지만.nuance: 하지만 is the standard, clear-cut 'but / however' for contrasting two full sentences, and it reads a touch more formal and decisive than 그런데/근데. The crucial contrast to internalize is 하지만 vs 그런데: 하지만 is purely contrastive — it never means 'by the way' and never changes the topic, whereas 그런데 is soft and frequently just pivots subjects. So if you only mean a plain 'but', 하지만 is the safe pick; if you're easing into a new question, you want 그런데. It is essentially the sentence-initial sibling of the connective -지만 (어렵지만 재미있어요 = 어려워요. 하지만 재미있어요). The pitfalls: never drop it into the middle of one sentence — it heads the contrasting sentence — and don't use it to mean 'by the way', which is 그런데's job, not 하지만's.
하지만.explanation: 하지만 (hajiman) = "but; however". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 하지만 ("but / however") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 하지만, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
하지만.shortExplanation: 하지만 means "but; however" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 하지만 to mean 'by the way' / to change topics. That nuance belongs only to 그런데; 하지만 is contrast and nothing else.
Splicing it mid-sentence: 맛있어요 하지만 비싸요. It must open the contrasting sentence — 맛있어요. 하지만 비싸요 (or one clause: 맛있지만 비싸요).
Stacking 하지만 with the clause ending -지만 at once: 어렵지만 하지만 재미있어요 is doubled-up. Pick one — either 어렵지만 재미있어요 or 어려워요. 하지만 재미있어요.

usagePhrases.note: Clean, direct contrast at the start of a sentence.
Interchangeable with 그렇지만 in almost every beginner sentence.

examples.en: Korean is hard. But it's really fun.
examples.note: The classic learner contrast sentence.

examples.ko: 저도 가고 싶었어요. 하지만 시간이 없었어요.
examples.romanization: jeodo gago sipeosseoyo. hajiman sigani eopseosseoyo.
examples.en: I wanted to go too. But I didn't have the time.
examples.note: Past wish vs past reality; both clauses keep their tense.

examples.ko: 발표는 떨렸어요. 하지만 끝까지 잘 해냈습니다.
examples.romanization: balpyoneun tteollyeosseoyo. hajiman kkeutkkaji jal haenaetseumnida.
examples.en: The presentation was nerve-wracking. However, I saw it through well.
examples.note: A notch more formal — fits a 합니다-style report.

cluster.title: 하지만 vs 그렇지만 vs 그래도
cluster.rule: 하지만 and 그렇지만 are both a plain "but" and swap freely — 하지만 is the one you'll hear more in speech, 그렇지만 sounds a touch more careful. Reach for 그래도 only when you mean "even so": you accept the fact and do it anyway.

example.en: Kimchi is spicy. But it's delicious.
Korean is difficult. But it's fun.
It's expensive. Even so, I'm going to buy it.

ex.en: It is a little inconvenient. However, it is possible.
ex.note: A slightly fuller form of 하지만.

그렇지만.nuance: 그렇지만 means 'but / however / nevertheless' and is the close sibling of 하지만 — in most beginner sentences they swap freely. It is literally 그렇- ('be so') + -지만 ('but'), so it carries a faint undertone of 'that may be true, but…', conceding the prior point a hair more than the flat 하지만. Register-wise it leans slightly more formal and polished, comfortable in writing or careful, polite speech (감사합니다. 그렇지만 사양하겠습니다). Set it against two neighbors: 그런데/근데 is the soft, casual 'but' that can also mean 'by the way', which 그렇지만 never does; and 그래도 is 'even so', a concessive 'I'll do it anyway' rather than a neutral 'however'. The pitfall is the same as for any of these connectors — it heads the contrasting sentence, so never bury it in the middle of one clause.
그렇지만.explanation: "but; however; nevertheless" is 그렇지만 (geureochiman). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 그렇지만 ("but / however"). Watch the particle attached to 그렇지만 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
그렇지만.shortExplanation: 그렇지만 means "but; however; nevertheless" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Burying it mid-sentence: 좋아요 그렇지만 비싸요. It opens the contrasting sentence — 좋아요. 그렇지만 비싸요 (or fuse to one clause: 좋지만 비싸요).
Expecting it to mean 'by the way' like 그런데. 그렇지만 is contrast only; for a topic change you need 그런데/근데.
Doubling it with -지만: 어렵지만 그렇지만 재미있어요 repeats the same 'but'. Use either 어렵지만 재미있어요 or 어려워요. 그렇지만 재미있어요.

usagePhrases.note: Clear contrast, a touch more formal than 하지만.
Softens with reassurance after a downside.
Nearly interchangeable; 그렇지만 carries a faint 'that may be so, but…'

examples.ko: 한국어 시험이 어려웠어요. 그렇지만 끝까지 포기하지 않았어요.
examples.romanization: hangugeo siheomi eoryeowosseoyo. geureochiman kkeutkkaji pogihaji anasseoyo.
examples.en: The Korean exam was hard. Nevertheless, I didn't give up to the end.
examples.note: Effort holding firm against difficulty.

examples.en: I appreciate the offer. However, I'll decline this time.
examples.note: Polite, formal refusal — register fits a workplace.

examples.ko: 증상은 가벼웠어요. 그렇지만 병원에 가 보기로 했어요.
examples.romanization: jeungsangeun gabyeowosseoyo. geureochiman byeongwone ga bogiro haesseoyo.
examples.en: The symptoms were mild. But still, I decided to see a doctor.
examples.note: Acknowledges one fact, takes a cautious turn.

cluster.title: 하지만 vs 그렇지만 vs 그래도
cluster.rule: 하지만 and 그렇지만 are both a plain "but" and swap freely — 하지만 is the one you'll hear more in speech, 그렇지만 sounds a touch more careful. Reach for 그래도 only when you mean "even so": you accept the fact and do it anyway.

example.en: Kimchi is spicy. But it's delicious.
Korean is difficult. But it's fun.
It's expensive. Even so, I'm going to buy it.

ex.en: It is expensive. Even so, shall we try going?
ex.note: 그래도 keeps the plan or feeling despite the previous sentence.

그래도.nuance: 그래도 means 'even so / but still' — you fully accept the previous fact, yet what follows defies what that fact would predict, carrying a flavor of perseverance or resolve. It is the sentence-initial partner of the concessive ending -아도/-어도 ('even if'); 비싸요. 그래도 사요 mirrors 비싸도 사요. The dangerous look-alike is 그래서 ('so / therefore'): one letter apart, opposite meaning — 그래서 follows the expected result, 그래도 goes AGAINST it. So 피곤해요. 그래서 자요 (tired, so I sleep) vs 피곤해요. 그래도 안 자요 (tired, but still I won't sleep). It also differs from plain contrast words like 하지만: 하지만 just sets two ideas side by side, while 그래도 specifically concedes 'granting all that…' and pushes through. Don't use it where there's no 'expected-vs-actual' gap; without that tension it sounds illogical.
그래도.explanation: 그래도 (geuraedo) = "still; even so; but still". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 그래도 ("still / even so") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 그래도, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
그래도.shortExplanation: 그래도 means "still; even so; but still" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Swapping it with 그래서: 피곤해요. 그래서 안 자요 is contradictory (tired, so I won't sleep?). To mean 'tired but still won't sleep' use 그래도 안 자요.
Using 그래도 with no real contrast: 맛있어요. 그래도 또 먹어요 makes no sense (no concession). It needs an 'against expectation' gap — e.g. 배불러요. 그래도 또 먹어요.
Stacking it redundantly with -아도: 추워도 그래도… is acceptable for emphasis but learners often double it wrongly. Either 추워도 산책해요 or 추워요. 그래도 산책해요 is cleaner.

usagePhrases.note: Grants the prior fact, then does the unexpected anyway.

usagePhrases.en: It's expensive. Even so, I'll buy it.
It's hard. But still, it's okay.
usagePhrases.note: Accepts the difficulty without giving up.
Polite thanks despite whatever just happened.

examples.en: It's cold out. Even so, I want to take a walk.
examples.note: Doing it anyway against expectation.

examples.ko: 많이 혼났어요. 그래도 후회는 안 해요.
examples.romanization: mani honnasseoyo. geuraedo huhoeneun an haeyo.
examples.en: I got scolded a lot. But still, I don't regret it.
examples.note: Concedes the cost, holds the stance.

examples.en: Even when I'm busy, I still always work out.
examples.note: Reinforces the concessive ending -아도/-어도 with 그래도.

cluster.title: 하지만 vs 그렇지만 vs 그래도
cluster.rule: 하지만 and 그렇지만 are both a plain "but" and swap freely — 하지만 is the one you'll hear more in speech, 그렇지만 sounds a touch more careful. Reach for 그래도 only when you mean "even so": you accept the fact and do it anyway.

example.en: Kimchi is spicy. But it's delicious.
Korean is difficult. But it's fun.
It's expensive. Even so, I'm going to buy it.

ex.en: Even if it is easy, you can make a mistake.
ex.note: 쉽다 becomes 쉬워도.

쉽다.nuance: 쉽다 is ㅂ irregular: 쉬워요, 쉬운. It helps learners talk about difficulty level, but the opposite 어렵다 is often needed in the same lesson.
쉽다.explanation: 쉽다 (swipda) = "to be easy". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 쉬워요 ("It is easy.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 쉽다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.
쉽다.shortExplanation: 쉽다 means "to be easy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
쉽다 becomes 쉬워요, not 쉽어요.

conjugationTips.title: Describing a noun: ㄴ/은 vs ㄹ/을
conjugationTips.body: To put 쉽다 in front of a noun, use the ㄴ/은 form for how something is right now: 쉬운 것 ("a easy thing"). The ㄹ/을 form points to something that will or might become that way later. So 뜨거운 물 is water that is hot now, but 뜨거울 물 is water that will be hot — same adjective, different time feeling. For everyday description, reach for the ㄴ/은 form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem: ㅂ → 우
conjugationTips.body: 쉽다 is a ㅂ-irregular word. Before a vowel ending the final ㅂ turns into 우, so the polite form is 쉬워요 — not a literal ㅂ + 어요. The same change gives the noun-describing form (맵다 → 매운, 쉽다 → 쉬운). Anchor on 쉬워요 and build the rest from it.

examples.en: This problem is easy.
examples.note: Topic.

examples.en: Korean is not easy.
examples.note: Careful negative.

examples.en: It is an easy sentence.
examples.note: Before noun.

ex.en: I will keep going even if it is hard.
ex.note: Often appears in concession sentences.

계속.nuance: 계속 means an action or state keeps going WITHOUT a break — 'continuously / the whole time / keep ~ing'. It's Sino-Korean 繼續 'connect-continue', which is exactly the image: things joined end to end with no gap. It can fuse with 하다 into the verb 계속하다 'to continue (something)' and appears as the connector 계속해서 'on and on'. The contrast to nail is 계속 vs 자꾸: 계속 is unbroken duration (비가 계속 와요 'it rains nonstop'), while 자꾸 is 'again and again, repeatedly' with gaps between tries, and usually carries a tinge of annoyance (자꾸 전화가 와요 'calls keep coming, ugh'). So 'the baby cried the whole time' is 계속 울었어요, but 'the baby kept waking up (on and off)' leans 자꾸 깼어요. Also distinguish the durative '-고 있다' (in progress right now) — 계속 stresses unbroken continuation over a stretch. No particle, before the verb; collocates with 오다, 가다, 하다, and direction verbs like 직진하다.
계속.explanation: 계속 (gyesok) = "continuously, keep ~ing". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 계속하세요 ("please continue") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 계속, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
계속.shortExplanation: 계속 means "continuously, keep ~ing" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 계속 (nonstop, unbroken) when you mean 'over and over' with mild irritation, e.g. on-and-off pestering. That intermittent, annoyed nuance is 자꾸: 자꾸 물어봐요 'they keep asking (and it's bugging me)'.
Saying 계속에 — no particle. Use bare 계속, or the verb 계속하다 / connector 계속해서.
Forgetting 계속 can take an object via 계속하다, e.g. 'continue the meeting' is 회의를 계속하다, not ✗ 회의를 계속 (adverb alone needs a following verb).

usagePhrases.note: 계속 + 하다 fused as a verb; common when telling someone to carry on.
Connected -아서 form for 'keep on (doing)' without a break.
Useful in directions: 계속 직진하세요 'keep going straight'.

examples.en: It keeps raining.
examples.note: Ongoing, unbroken action; 계속 before the verb.

examples.en: If you keep going straight here, you'll reach the subway station.
examples.note: 계속 + 직진하다 in real directions — 'continuously, without turning'.

examples.ko: 아기가 자꾸 깨서 밤새 계속 안아 줬어요.
examples.romanization: agiga jakku kkaeseo bamsae gyesok ana jwosseoyo.
examples.en: The baby kept waking up, so I held her all night long.
examples.note: Contrasts 자꾸 (over and over, intermittently) with 계속 (the whole time, unbroken).

ex.en: There are drawbacks too, but there are more advantages.
ex.note: Pairs naturally with 단점.

장점.nuance: 장점 is Sino-Korean (長點, 長 'long/superior' + 點 'point'), literally a 'strong point' — a merit, advantage, or strength of a thing, plan, or person. It is almost always used in deliberate contrast with its antonym 단점 (短點, 'short point' = weakness/drawback); the pair 장점과 단점 is a fixed collocation, like English 'pros and cons'. Compare 장점 with 강점 (強點, 'strong point/forte'): 강점 emphasizes a competitive strength relative to others (우리 회사의 강점 = our company's competitive edge), while 장점 is the neutral 'good point' of anything. Also note 좋은 점 (a more colloquial 'the good thing about it'). Register-neutral and common in reviews, interviews, and comparisons. Collocations: 장점이 있다/많다, 장점을 살리다 (leverage), 장점을 살펴보다 (examine the merits), 큰 장점, 최대 장점 (greatest advantage). The English-speaker pitfall: don't translate 'advantage' as 이득 or 이점 indiscriminately — 이득 (利得) is material 'gain/profit', and 이점 (利點) is 'an advantageous point/benefit' often in a strategic sense; for the everyday 'good point of X', 장점 is the natural choice. Also, when describing a person's virtue, 장점 (good trait) differs from 매력 (charm/appeal) — a reliable friend has a 장점, a charismatic one has 매력.
장점.explanation: 장점 (jangjeom) = "strength, merit, advantage". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 장점이 있다 ("to have a merit/strength") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 장점, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
장점.shortExplanation: 장점 means "strength, merit, advantage" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Pairing the wrong antonym: the opposite of 장점 is 단점 (장점과 단점 = pros and cons), not 약점 (which is 'a vulnerability/weak spot', e.g. in a fight or argument).
Using 이득 for 'advantage' of a method — 이득 is monetary gain; the merit/strength of a plan is its 장점.
Saying 장점이 좋다 — that's redundant ('the good point is good'); just say 장점이 있다/많다, or 좋은 점이 있다.

usagePhrases.note: 장점 + 이 with 있다, an advantage exists
장점 + 이 with 많다, lots of good points
가장 큰 + 장점, ranking the top merit

usagePhrases.en: to make the most of a strength
usagePhrases.note: 장점 + 을 with 살리다, to leverage an advantage

examples.en: This method has many advantages.
examples.note: Simple frame: subject + 장점이 많다/있다 to list what's good about something.

examples.ko: 온라인 수업의 장점은 시간을 아낄 수 있다는 거예요.
examples.romanization: ollain sueobui jangjeomeun siganeul akkil su itdaneun geoyeyo.
examples.en: The advantage of online classes is that you can save time.
examples.note: Everyday frame: ~의 장점은 ...라는 것이다, the set 'the advantage of X is that ~' pattern.

examples.ko: 면접에서 자신의 장점과 단점을 솔직하게 말하는 게 좋아요.
examples.romanization: myeonjeobeseo jasinui jangjeomgwa danjeomeul soljikage malhaneun ge joayo.
examples.en: In an interview, it's good to honestly state your own strengths and weaknesses.
examples.note: Real situation: 장점과 단점 paired in the classic interview question about yourself.

ex.en: Even if there is a drawback, I am okay with it.
ex.note: Useful with -아/어도.

단점.nuance: 단점 is Sino-Korean (短點, 短 'short/lacking' + 點 'point'), literally a 'short point' — a weakness, drawback, flaw, or shortcoming of a thing, plan, or person. It is the fixed antonym of 장점 (長點, merit), and the pair 장점과 단점 functions exactly like English 'pros and cons / strengths and weaknesses'. The key contrast to master is 단점 vs 약점 (弱點, 'weak point/vulnerability'): 단점 is a general flaw or downside that's just part of something (이 차의 단점 = this car's drawback, e.g. poor mileage), while 약점 is an exploitable vulnerability or sensitive spot — a rival attacks your 약점, a coach targets the opponent's 약점, and a personal sore subject is a 약점, not a 단점. Also compare 결점 (缺點, a 'defect/fault', slightly stronger, hints at something missing) and 흠 (a native word for a 'flaw/blemish'). Register-neutral. Collocations: 단점이 있다/없다, 단점을 고치다/보완하다 (fix/compensate), 단점을 인정하다 (admit a flaw), 큰 단점. The English-speaker pitfall: in self-introductions, 'my weakness' should be 단점 (a manageable shortcoming), not 약점 — calling it your 약점 sounds like you're confessing an exploitable vulnerability. And don't say 단점이 나쁘다 ('the drawback is bad') — that's redundant; just 단점이 있다.
단점.explanation: 단점 (danjeom) means "weakness, drawback, shortcoming". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 단점이 있다 ("to have a drawback"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 단점 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
단점.shortExplanation: 단점 means "weakness, drawback, shortcoming" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying your interview 'weakness' is your 약점 — use 단점 (a shortcoming); 약점 is an exploitable vulnerability/sore spot, which sounds wrong in self-introduction.
Mismatching the antonym: 단점 pairs with 장점 (단점보다 장점이 많다 = more pros than cons), not with 강점.
Adding a redundant evaluation: 단점이 나쁘다 is circular; say 단점이 있다, or name it: 단점은 비싸다는 거예요 (the drawback is that it's expensive).

usagePhrases.note: 단점 + 이 with 있다, a weak point exists
단점 + 을 with 고치다, to improve a flaw
가장 큰 + 단점, ranking the worst weakness

usagePhrases.en: to make up for a weakness
usagePhrases.note: 단점 + 을 with 보완하다, to compensate for a flaw

examples.en: This phone has almost no drawbacks.
examples.note: Simple frame: subject + 단점이 없다/있다 to evaluate the downsides of a product.

examples.ko: 제 단점은 가끔 너무 솔직하다는 거예요.
examples.romanization: je danjeomeun gakkeum neomu soljikadaneun geoyeyo.
examples.en: My weakness is that I'm sometimes too honest.
examples.note: Everyday frame: ~의 단점은 ...라는 것이다, the 'my weakness is that ~' interview pattern.

examples.ko: 이 방법의 단점은 시간이 오래 걸린다는 점인데, 그래도 가장 안전해요.
examples.romanization: i bangbeobui danjeomeun sigani orae geollindaneun jeominde, geuraedo gajang anjeonhaeyo.
examples.en: The drawback of this method is that it takes a long time, but it's still the safest.
examples.note: Real situation: conceding a 단점 (~다는 점) while still recommending the option.

ex.en: It is a little inconvenient, but possible.
ex.note: A realistic planning contrast.

불편하다.nuance: 불편하다 fronts the Sino-Korean negative prefix 不 (불, 'not') onto 便 (편, 'convenient'), literally 'not-convenient', and is the all-purpose antonym of 편하다. It covers physical discomfort (tight shoes, a hard bed), practical inconvenience (poor transport, a clunky process), social unease (feeling awkward around someone), and gently, being unwell or physically impaired (몸이 불편하다 is the courteous phrase for illness or disability). It is the polite backbone of complaints — service desks ask 불편한 점이 있으셨어요? ('was anything inconvenient?'). Boundary note: 불편하다 is the broad 'uncomfortable/inconvenient', while 어색하다 zeroes in on the awkward unfamiliarity between people who aren't close, and 아프다 is plain physical pain. As a 하다 adjective it conjugates to 불편해요. English-speaker pitfall: the literal calque 안 편하다 is understood but sounds like a learner workaround — the natural single lexical antonym is 불편하다; and don't use 불편하다 for sharp pain, which is 아파요.
불편하다.explanation: 불편하다 (bulpyeonhada) means "to be uncomfortable; inconvenient". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 불편해요 ("It's uncomfortable / inconvenient"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 불편하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
불편하다.shortExplanation: 불편하다 means "to be uncomfortable; inconvenient" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying the calque 안 편하다 — it is understood but the natural single word is 불편하다.
Conjugating as 불편하요; 하다 adjectives take 해요, giving 불편해요.
Using 불편하다 for sharp physical pain — that is 아파요; 불편하다 is discomfort/inconvenience, or a soft word for being unwell.

usagePhrases.en: I feel unwell / my body is impaired
