Distinguish it from 그만두다, which is 'to quit/stop' an ongoing activity or job (회사를 그만두다, 'quit the company'; 운동을 그만두다, 'stop exercising'): you 취소해요 a future arrangement, but you 그만둬요 something already in progress. It also differs from 미루다 ('postpone', 약속을 미루다, push the appointment later rather than scrap it) — canceling removes it, postponing reschedules it. As a noun+하다 verb it's regular: 취소하 + 여요 → 취소해요, past 취소했어요, with 안/못 before 하다 (취소 안 해요, 취소 못 해요). English-speaker pitfall: 'cancel my subscription / unsubscribe' is more often 해지하다 (解止, end a contract) than 취소하다, and don't use 취소하다 for 'quit a job' — that's 그만두다.
취소하다.explanation: 취소하다 (chwisohada) = "to cancel". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 취소해요 plus one useful sentence like 예약을 취소하다 ("to cancel a reservation"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 취소하고 싶어요 for what you want, 취소할 수 있어요 for what you can, 취소 못 해요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
취소하다.shortExplanation: 취소하다 means "to cancel" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 취소하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 취소해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 취소하다 for 'quit a job/activity' — quitting something ongoing is 그만두다; 취소하다 calls off a future arrangement (booking, order, plan).
Confusing 취소하다 with 미루다 — canceling removes the plan, but 미루다 only postpones it: 약속을 미뤘어요 ('I pushed it back').
Saying 못 취소해요 — the noun+하다 negative is 취소 못 해요 / 취소 안 해요 (split goes before 하다).

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 취소하다 becomes 취소할 수 있어요 ("can") and 취소할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: 취소하다 undoes a booking/order; 예약을 취소해요

examples.en: I cancel the reservation.
examples.note: Noun+하다 compound, regular: stem 취소하 + 여요 → 취소해요

examples.en: Something came up, so I canceled the appointment.
examples.note: 일이 생기다 = 'something comes up'; -아서 gives the reason; past 취소했어요

examples.ko: 이미 결제해서 지금은 취소 못 해요.
examples.romanization: imi gyeoljehaeseo jigeumeun chwiso mo taeyo.
examples.en: I already paid, so I can't cancel now.
examples.note: 이미 ('already') + past reason; 못 splits as 취소 못 해요

ex.en: I got a phone call.
ex.note: The incoming call can interrupt an action.

받다.nuance: 받다 is for receiving things, messages, help, service, or documents.
받다.explanation: "to receive" in Korean is 받다 (batda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 받아요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 받다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 문자를 받아요 ("receive a text.") — then reshape the same stem into 받고 싶어요 (desire), 받을 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 받아요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
받다.shortExplanation: 받다 means "to receive" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 받다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 받아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
받아 주세요 often means “please accept/take this,” not simply “please receive” in an abstract way.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 받다 becomes 받을 수 있어요 ("can") and 받을 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

examples.en: I received a text.
examples.note: Past.

examples.en: Can I get a receipt?
examples.note: Shopping.

examples.en: I want to receive help.
examples.note: Need help.

ex.en: People are standing in line.
ex.note: 서 있다 describes a continuing posture or line state.

서다.nuance: 서다 means to stand or, for vehicles, to come to a stop. Because the stem already ends in 어, the 요-ending merges instead of doubling: you get 서요 and the past 섰어요, never 서어요 or 서었어요. Watch the two sister verbs: 서다 is the plain state/result 'to be standing / take a standing position', while 일어서다 ('rise to one's feet') stresses the motion of getting up from sitting — so 'please stand up (from your seat)' is 일어서 주세요, but 'please stand here' is 여기 서 주세요. For vehicles 서다 overlaps with 멈추다 ('to halt'); 멈추다 is more general and can describe machines or actions stopping, while 서다 is the everyday word for a bus or car pulling up. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: the location where you stand takes 에 (여기에 서다), not the object marker, and don't say 줄에 서다 — the idiom is 줄을 서다, treating the line as something you 'do'. Korean also has no separate verb for 'stand something up'; that meaning needs the causative 세우다.
서다.explanation: 서다 (seoda) = "to stand". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 서요 plus one useful sentence like 여기 서 주세요 ("Please stand here"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 서고 싶어요 for what you want, 설 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 서요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
서다.shortExplanation: 서다 means "to stand" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 서다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 서요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing the doubled 서어요/서었어요 — since the stem ends in 어, it contracts with the ending, so the correct forms are 서요 and 섰어요.
Saying 줄에 서요 for 'stand in line' — the natural idiom treats the line as an object, so it must be 줄을 서요/줄을 섰어요.
Using 서다 to mean 'stand something upright' (e.g., 'I stood the bottle on the table') — 서다 is intransitive; for that you need the causative 세우다, as in 병을 세웠어요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 서다 becomes 설 수 있어요 ("can") and 설 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: the spot where you stand takes 에 (여기에), often dropped in speech

examples.en: Please stand in front of the door.
examples.note: place + 에 marks where you take your standing position

examples.en: People formed a long line.
examples.note: 줄을 서다 is the set phrase for queuing; 섰어요 is the contracted past

examples.en: The taxi suddenly stopped in front of us.
examples.note: same verb = a vehicle coming to a halt

ex.en: The door is open.
ex.note: The open state remains.

열리다.nuance: 열다 needs an actor opening something. 열리다 lets the opened thing become the subject.
열리다.explanation: 열리다 (yeollida) = "to open; to be opened". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 문이 열려 있어요. ("The door is open.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 열리다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
열리다.shortExplanation: 열리다 means "to open; to be opened" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not say 문을 열려 있어요. The thing in the state takes 이/가: 문이 열려 있어요.
Use 열고 있어요 only when someone is actively opening it right now.

usagePhrases.note: The window became open and remains that way.

examples.en: The cafe door is still open.
examples.note: 아직 plus result-state is very natural.

켜지다.en: to turn on; to be on

ex.en: The light is on.
ex.note: The on-state remains.

켜지다.nuance: 켜다 is the action of turning something on. 켜지다 focuses on the thing becoming or being on.
켜지다.explanation: 켜지다 (kyeojida) means "to turn on; to be turned on". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 불이 켜져 있어요. ("The light is on."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 켜지다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
켜지다.shortExplanation: 켜지다 means "to turn on; to be turned on" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not say 불을 켜져 있어요. Say 불이 켜져 있어요.
Use 켜고 있어요 only when someone is in the act of turning it on.

examples.ko: 방에 불이 켜져 있어서 누가 있는 줄 알았어요.
examples.romanization: bange buri kyeojyeo isseoseo nuga inneun jul arasseoyo.
examples.en: The light was on in the room, so I thought someone was there.
examples.note: Result-state gives the visual clue.

ex.en: The door is in an open state.
ex.note: Names the state directly.

상태.nuance: 상태 (狀態, 狀 'shape/form' + 態 'condition') is the present condition of one specific thing — a person's health, an object, a system — captured at a moment. The sharp contrast is 상태 vs 상황: 상태 zooms in on the CONDITION of a single entity (건강 상태 'health condition'), while 상황 is the broader CIRCUMSTANCE/situation surrounding events (교통 상황 'traffic situation', 지금 상황이 복잡해요). Habitual partners: 상태가 좋다/나쁘다, 상태를 확인하다, 건강/배터리/도로 상태, ~한 상태 ('in a … state'). A handy grammar use: 술에 취한 상태로 = 'in a drunken state.' The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: 'the condition is good' is 상태가 좋다 ✓ (좋다 descriptive), never 상태를 좋다 ✗; and don't reach for 상황 when you mean one thing's condition.
상태.explanation: "state; condition" is 상태 (sangtae). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 상태가 좋아요 ("the condition is good"). Watch the particle attached to 상태 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
상태.shortExplanation: 상태 means "state; condition" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 상태를 좋다 ✗ — 좋다 describes a state, so the particle is 가: 상태가 좋다 ✓
Using 상황 (broad situation) when you mean the condition of one specific thing → 상태
Forgetting the compound has no particle: it is 건강 상태, not 건강의 상태 in everyday speech

examples.en: The condition is good.
examples.note: simplest state sentence with 가

examples.ko: 요즘 잠을 못 자서 건강 상태가 안 좋아요.
examples.romanization: yojeum jameul mot jaseo geongang sangtaega an joayo.
examples.en: I haven't slept well lately, so my health condition isn't good.
examples.note: 건강 상태 + 안 좋다 (negated state)

examples.ko: 중고차라서 사기 전에 상태를 꼼꼼히 확인했어요.
examples.romanization: junggocharaseo sagi jeone sangtaereul kkomkkomhi hwaginhaesseoyo.
examples.en: Since it's a used car, I checked its condition carefully before buying.
examples.note: real-situation: 상태를 확인하다 about a physical object

ex.en: The road was jammed. So I was a little late.
ex.note: Use 그래서 after the cause has already been stated.

그래서.nuance: 그래서 links a cause to its natural result — 'so / that's why' — and is the first cause-effect connector a beginner must own. It is the sentence-starting cousin of the clause ending -아서/-어서 (피곤해서 일찍 자요 = 피곤해요. 그래서 일찍 자요). The sharp boundary to learn is 그래서 vs 그러니까: both can mean 'so', but 그래서 reports a plain consequence, while 그러니까 pushes a conclusion onto the listener and is what you use before a command or suggestion (피곤하지? 그러니까 일찍 자 = so go to bed). Two real pitfalls: first, 그래서 cannot head an imperative or a let's-form — 그래서 일찍 자세요 sounds off, so switch to 그러니까. Second, English 'so' can also mean 'very' ('so tired'); that meaning is 너무/정말, never 그래서. Keep 그래서 strictly for result.
그래서.explanation: 그래서 (geuraeseo) means "so; therefore". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 그래서 ("so / that's why"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 그래서 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
그래서.shortExplanation: 그래서 means "so; therefore" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 그래서 before a command: 비가 와요. 그래서 우산 가져가세요. Result-into-an-order needs 그러니까 — 비가 와요. 그러니까 우산 가져가세요.
Mixing it up with 그런데 (but / by the way). 그래서 = result; 그런데 = mild contrast or topic shift. They are not interchangeable.
Translating 'so tired' as 그래서 피곤해요. There 'so' means 'very', so it should be 너무 피곤해요; 그래서 only means 'therefore'.

usagePhrases.note: Points back to the previous sentence and names its result.

usagePhrases.en: I'm tired. So I sleep early.

usagePhrases.note: Casual nudge for the speaker to get to the point.

usagePhrases.en: So how did it turn out?
usagePhrases.note: Stock follow-up that asks for the outcome of a story.

examples.en: It's raining. So I'm taking an umbrella.
examples.note: Plain cause → everyday result.

examples.ko: 어제 늦게 잤어요. 그래서 오늘 너무 피곤해요.
examples.romanization: eoje neutge jasseoyo. geuraeseo oneul neomu pigonhaeyo.
examples.en: I went to bed late yesterday. So I'm exhausted today.
examples.note: Past reason leading to a present state — both verbs carry their own tense.

examples.ko: 길이 막혔어요. 그래서 회의에 늦었어요. 죄송합니다.
examples.romanization: giri makyeosseoyo. geuraeseo hoeuie neujeosseoyo. joesonghamnida.
examples.en: Traffic was jammed. So I was late to the meeting. I'm sorry.
examples.note: Real apology context — 그래서 supplies the excuse.

cluster.title: 그리고 vs 그래서 vs 그런데 vs 그러면
cluster.rule: Pick by the logical link back to the sentence you just said: 그리고 simply adds, 그래서 gives its result, 그런데 turns away from it, and 그러면 treats it as a premise ("if that's so, then…"). Note that in real speech 그런데/근데 is very often not contrast at all — it's just "by the way", a way to slide into a new topic.

example.en: I had dinner. And then I drank coffee.
It's raining. So I'm staying home.

members.when: soft contrast, or changing the topic

example.en: By the way, when are we meeting?

members.en: then, in that case, if so
members.when: reacting to what was just said

막히다.en: to be blocked; to be jammed

ex.en: The road was jammed, so I was late to the appointment.
ex.note: The subject is 길 or 차, not the late person.

막히다.nuance: 막히다 is the passive/intransitive partner of the transitive 막다 ('to block'): the -히- infix turns 'someone blocks X' into 'X gets blocked', so 막히다 is something that HAPPENS to a road, drain, or nose rather than something you do. For traffic this is the single most useful verb — 길이 막히다 / 차가 막히다 — and its opposite is 뚫리다 ('to open up/clear'), with 안 막히다 the everyday 'no traffic'. Do not confuse it with 막다 itself: 'I block the road' is 길을 막다, but 'the road is jammed' is 길이 막히다, and the particle flips from 을 to 이/가 accordingly. Register is plain and universal. Because the subject is a non-person, the polite/imperative-looking forms (막혀 주세요, 막힐까요?) are essentially never used about traffic. The big English-speaker trap is treating it as transitive: there is no 'I am blocked by traffic' with you as subject — Korean puts the ROAD in the subject slot (길이 막혀요), and you simply say 길이 막혀서 늦었어요 ('I was late because the road was jammed').
막히다.explanation: 막히다 (makhi-da) = "to be blocked". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 막혀요 plus one useful sentence like 길이 막히다 ("for the road to be congested"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 막히고 싶어요 for what you want, 막힐 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 막혀요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off.
막히다.shortExplanation: 막히다 means "to be blocked" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 막히다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 막혀요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 저는 막혀요 to mean 'I'm stuck in traffic'. 막히다 takes the ROAD as subject, not the person: 길이 막혀요, then 그래서 늦었어요.
Mixing up 막다 and 막히다. 길을 막다 = 'to block the road (actively)'; 길이 막히다 = 'the road is congested'. Watch the particle: 을 for the active verb, 이/가 for the passive one.
Using 막히다 for a person standing in your way. A person blocking you is 길을 막다 (they actively block) or 앞을 가로막다; 막히다 is reserved for roads, pipes, and noses.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 막히다 becomes 막힐 수 있어요 ("can") and 막힐 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.en: for the road to be congested
usagePhrases.note: 길 + 이 막히다 is THE everyday way to say 'traffic is bad'

examples.en: The road is congested.
examples.note: Core frame: 길 takes subject 이, the verb is intransitive

examples.en: The road was very jammed because it was rush hour.
examples.note: Everyday: 퇴근 시간이라 'because it's leaving-work time' gives the cause

examples.ko: 지금 출발하면 차가 막혀서 두 시간 걸릴 거예요.
examples.romanization: jigeum chulbalhamyeon chaga makyeoseo du sigan geollil geoyeyo.
examples.en: If you leave now traffic will be bad and it'll take two hours.
examples.note: Real situation: 막혀서 chains cause to the 걸리다 'take time' result

ex.ko: 버스가 고장 나는 바람에 오래 기다렸어요.
ex.en: The bus broke down, so I waited for a long time.
ex.note: A strong 바람에 cause because the problem was not planned.

ex.en: I missed the bus, so I was late to class.
ex.note: 놓치다 often creates an unwanted result.

놓치다.nuance: 놓치다 is for missing something you were actively trying to catch or hold — a bus, a train, a flight, a chance, or even the thread of a conversation (요점을 놓치다 = 'miss the point') — and it always takes a 을/를 object. Its make-up shows the meaning: 놓다 ('to let go/release') + 치다, so it literally pictures something slipping out of your grasp. The single biggest English-speaker pitfall is using it for missing a *person*: English 'I miss you' is NOT 놓치다 — that is 보고 싶다 ('want to see'), so 엄마가 보고 싶어요, never 엄마를 놓쳐요. Contrast 놓치다 ('fail to catch what was within reach') with 지나가다/지나치다 ('let pass / pass by'): you 놓치다 a bus you ran for, but a chance that quietly 지나가다 simply went by. It is a regular ㅣ-stem verb: 놓치 + 어 → 놓쳐요, and it frequently appears alongside 늦다 ('be late').
놓치다.explanation: 놓치다 (nochida) = "to miss". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 놓쳐요 plus one useful sentence like 버스를 놓쳤어요 ("I missed the bus"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 놓치고 싶어요 for what you want, 놓칠 수 있어요 for what you can, 놓칠 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
놓치다.shortExplanation: 놓치다 means "to miss" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 놓치다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 놓쳐요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
To say you miss a PERSON, use 보고 싶다, not 놓치다 — 놓치다 is only for missing a bus, train, chance, etc.
Don't drop the object marker: it's 버스를 놓쳤어요, since 놓치다 is transitive and needs a 을/를 object.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 놓치다 becomes 놓칠 수 있어요 ("can") and 놓칠 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: 놓치다 = fail to catch a bus/train/flight; the thing missed takes 을/를.

examples.en: I just missed the bus
examples.note: The most typical use, for transport you failed to catch.

examples.en: I was late because I missed the subway
examples.note: Pairs naturally with 늦다 in everyday excuses (-아서 gives the reason).

examples.ko: 이런 좋은 기회를 놓치면 안 돼요
examples.romanization: ireon joeun gihoereul notchimyeon an dwaeyo
examples.en: You shouldn't miss a good chance like this
examples.note: Opportunities use 놓치다 too; -면 안 되다 gives the 'mustn't' warning.

ex.en: We moved the gathering to next week.
ex.note: A natural result when everyone is late or the weather is bad.

모임.nuance: 모임 is native Korean, built from the verb 모이다 'to gather/come together' plus the noun-forming -ㅁ, so it literally means 'a gathering.' It is the broadest, most neutral word for people coming together for a shared purpose — a club, a reunion, a regular dinner crew — and unlike 파티 it carries no festive or Western flavor. The sharp contrast: 파티 is fun and event-like; 회식 is specifically a work-team meal; 모임 is the umbrella term that can be any of these in a low-key way, including serious or hobby groups (독서 모임 'book club', 동창 모임 'alumni reunion'). Particle logic mirrors other event nouns: 에 to attend (모임에 가요/나가요) and 이 to say one exists (모임이 있어요). The English-speaker pitfall is again 에서 with 가다 (모임에서 가요 ✗) — use 에 for the destination. A subtler point: because 모임 can name the standing group, 모임을 만들다 'form a group' is fine, whereas the same phrase sounds odd with one-off 파티.
모임.explanation: "gathering; meeting" is 모임 (moim). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 모임에 나가다 ("to attend / show up to a gathering"). Watch the particle attached to 모임 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
모임.shortExplanation: 모임 means "gathering; meeting" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 모임에서 가요 to mean 'go to the gathering' — 에서 marks where an action happens; the destination needs 에, so 모임에 가요/나가요.
Forcing the English word 'party' onto every 모임 — a quiet hobby club or reunion is a 모임, not a 파티; choosing 파티 makes it sound like a festive event it isn't.
Using 하다 for joining (모임을 해요 to mean 'I attend') — to attend, use 모임에 나가다/가다; 모임을 하다 means the group itself meets/holds a session.

usagePhrases.en: to attend / show up to a gathering
usagePhrases.note: 나가다 'go out (to)' is the idiomatic verb for joining a regular group meeting

usagePhrases.en: to have a gathering (on the schedule)
usagePhrases.note: 이 marks 모임 as the thing that exists; 오늘 모임이 있어요
unlike 파티, 모임 CAN take 만들다 because you create the standing group itself
the qualifier (가족, 동창, 독서) tells you who gathers

examples.en: I have a gathering today.
examples.note: simple: 있다 + 이 to state that a get-together is on the schedule

examples.ko: 저는 한 달에 한 번 독서 모임에 나가요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun han dare han beon dokseo moime nagayo.
examples.en: I attend a book club once a month.
examples.note: everyday: 나가다 is the go-to verb for a recurring 모임; 독서 모임 = reading gathering

examples.en: I started a small group with my friends.
examples.note: real-situation: here 모임 is the standing club you create, so 만들다 'make' is correct

ex.en: The road was jammed because of an accident.
ex.note: A concrete noun cause for N 때문에.

사고.nuance: 사고 (事故, 'matter-incident') covers any sudden harmful event — car crashes, workplace mishaps, falls — and is the umbrella word a 교통사고 or 산업재해 sits under. The make-or-break contrast is purely grammatical and Koreans listen for it: 사고가 나다 (with 가) means the accident merely HAPPENED, assigning no blame, while 사고를 내다 (with 를) means the subject CAUSED it and is therefore liable — get the particle wrong and you may accidentally confess fault at the scene. Compare also 사건, which is an 'incident/case' in the investigative or criminal sense (a 살인 사건 is a murder CASE), whereas 사고 leans toward unintended mishap. Natural partners are 교통사고, 사고가 나다/내다, 사고 현장, and the everyday 접촉사고 (a minor fender-bender).
사고.explanation: 사고 (sago) = "accident". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 교통사고 ("traffic accident") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 사고, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
사고.shortExplanation: 사고 means "accident" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't mix up 사고가 났어요 (an accident happened) with 사고를 냈어요 (I caused one) — the 를 version admits liability and your insurer will treat it differently.
사고 is the EVENT, not the people; the injured person is a 피해자 and the at-fault driver a 가해자 — never call a person a 사고.
Don't reach for 사건 when you mean an everyday crash; 사건 implies a criminal/investigative 'case', while a road bump is a 사고 (or 접촉사고).

usagePhrases.note: The single most common compound; written as one solid word, 交通事故.
나다 is the intransitive 'occur' — nobody is blamed, it just happened.
내다 (transitive 'bring about') marks the subject as the one at fault.
現場 'present-spot' = the exact place it happened; police seal it off.

examples.en: There's an accident up ahead.
examples.note: Bare frame: 사고가 나다, the neutral 'an accident occurred', nobody blamed yet.

examples.en: I caused an accident, so I called the insurance company.
examples.note: 사고를 내다 openly admits fault; the 가/를 swap is the whole meaning.

examples.en: If there's an accident, report it to 112 first.
examples.note: 112 is the police line; 119 is fire/ambulance — memorize both.

ex.en: I came in order to learn Korean.
ex.note: 배우기 위해서 is the purpose frame.

배우다.nuance: 배우다 means 'to learn / acquire a skill or subject' and takes the object marker 을/를: 한국어를 배워요. It is a regular verb, but the stem ends in the vowel 우, so when 어요 attaches the two vowels contract into 워 — 배우 + 어요 → 배워요 (not 배우어요), past 배웠어요. The natural partner verb is 가르치다 ('to teach'), the giving side of the same act; and the person you learn from takes 한테/에게서 (사람) — 선생님한테 배워요 — never the place particle 에서 for the source. Contrast 배우다 with 공부하다 (工夫하다, 'to study'): 공부하다 is the effort of studying (sitting down, reviewing, hitting the books), while 배우다 is the result of acquiring a skill or being taught it, often from someone. So you 공부하다 for an exam at your desk but 배우다 the piano from a teacher. The English-speaker pitfall is writing the uncontracted 배우어요, and saying 학원에서 배우다 to mean 'learn from the academy' — 에서 marks where, while the human source must take 한테/에게서.
배우다.explanation: 배우다 (baeuda) = "to learn". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 배워요 plus one useful sentence like 한국어를 배워요 ("I learn Korean"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 배우고 싶어요 for what you want, 배울 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 배워요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help.
배우다.shortExplanation: 배우다 means "to learn" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 배우다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 배워요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing the uncontracted 배우어요 — the 우 + 어요 contracts, so the polite present is 배워요 (past 배웠어요).
Confusing 배우다 with 공부하다 — 공부하다 is the act of studying/reviewing; 배우다 is acquiring or being taught a skill. Use 시험공부를 해요 for exam prep, 피아노를 배워요 for taking lessons.
Marking the person you learn from with 에서 — a human source takes 한테/에게서: 선생님한테 배워요, not 선생님에서.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 배우다 becomes 배울 수 있어요 ("can") and 배울 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: the subject/skill learned takes the object marker 을/를

examples.en: I learn Korean.
examples.note: two vowels contract: 배우 + 어요 → 배워요

examples.en: These days I'm learning guitar from a friend.
examples.note: source person takes 한테; 고 있다 = ongoing

examples.ko: 저는 운전을 배워서 회사에 차로 가고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun unjeoneul baewoseo hoesae charo gago sipeoyo.
examples.en: I want to learn to drive and go to work by car.
examples.note: real goal-linked sentence; 배워서 connects reason to plan

ex.en: I practice Korean in order to get a job.
ex.note: Noun plus 을 위해서.

취업.nuance: 취업 is the process or result of getting employment. 직업 is your occupation or job type, and 회사 is the company. For a purpose sentence, 취업을 위해서 or 취업하기 위해서 is natural.
취업.explanation: "employment; getting a job" is 취업 (chwieop). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 취업을 위해서 ("for employment / in order to get a job"). Watch the particle attached to 취업 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.
취업.shortExplanation: 취업 means "employment; getting a job" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 직업을 위해서 when you mean 'to get a job'. Use 취업을 위해서 or 취업하기 위해서.
Do not drop the object particle in the learner frame. Say 취업을 위해서, not 취업 위해서, until the full pattern feels natural.

usagePhrases.en: for employment / in order to get a job

usagePhrases.note: Common compound for preparing to get hired.

usagePhrases.en: to succeed in getting a job

examples.en: I practice Korean every day in order to get a job.
examples.note: Purpose plus daily practice.

examples.ko: 방학 동안 취업 준비를 할 거예요.
examples.romanization: banghak dongan chwieop junbireul hal geoyeyo.
examples.en: I will prepare for job hunting during vacation.
examples.note: Duration plus practical goal.

ex.en: I prepare in order to pass the exam.
ex.note: 합격하다 becomes 합격하기.

합격하다.nuance: 합격하다 is Sino-Korean 合格 — 合 'meet/match' + 格 'standard' — literally 'meet the standard', i.e. clear a cut-off and pass a test, interview, or admissions screen. Its opposite is 불합격하다 (不合格) or, much more colloquially, 떨어지다 'to fall/drop' (시험에 떨어졌어요 = I failed/flunked). Don't confuse 합격하다 with 통과하다 'to pass through': 통과하다 is moving past a checkpoint or a bill passing, while 합격하다 specifically means meeting a qualifying standard. The headline English-speaker pitfall is the particle: English 'pass THE exam' (object) makes learners write 시험을 합격하다, but Korean uses 에 — 시험에 합격하다 — because you're 'matching up TO the standard'. Note also 합격하다 (verb) vs 합격 (the noun, 'a pass/acceptance'): the noun is what you put on banners — 합격 축하해! As a noun+하다 verb it conjugates on 하다 (합격해요, 합격했어요, formal 합격합니다); negative/impossible split the noun (합격 안 해요, 합격 못 해요).
합격하다.explanation: "to pass an exam" in Korean is 합격하다 (hapgyeokada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 합격해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 합격하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 시험에 합격하다 ("to pass the exam / make the cut") — then reshape the same stem into 합격하고 싶어요 (desire), 합격할 수 있어요 (ability), and 합격 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
합격하다.shortExplanation: 합격하다 means "to pass an exam" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 합격하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 합격해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 시험을 합격했어요 because English treats the exam as a direct object — Korean marks it with 에: 시험에 합격했어요.
Using 합격하다 to mean a course or class 'passed' in the sense of finishing it — for clearing a checkpoint generally use 통과하다; 합격하다 = meeting a qualifying standard.
Forming 'I failed' as 합격 안 했어요, which sounds oddly neutral ('didn't pass') — the natural opposite Koreans say is 떨어졌어요 (시험에 떨어졌어요).

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 합격하다 becomes 합격할 수 있어요 ("can") and 합격할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not pass an exam.
I want to pass an exam.
I have to pass an exam.
to pass the exam / make the cut
usagePhrases.note: what you pass takes 에: 시험에 합격해요 (NOT 시험을)

examples.en: I passed the exam!
examples.note: Use 에 for the thing passed; the past 합격했어요 reports the result

examples.en: This time I really want to pass.
examples.note: 꼭 = for sure/without fail; 이번에는 = this time around

examples.ko: 공부를 안 하면 합격 못 해요.
examples.romanization: gongbureul an hamyeon hapgyeong mo taeyo.
examples.en: If you don't study, you can't pass.
examples.note: ~면 = if; impossible form splits: 합격 못 해요

ex.ko: 시험을 위해서 한 달 동안 준비했어요.
ex.en: I prepared for the exam for one month.
ex.note: A noun goal plus a duration.

시험.nuance: 시험 is Sino-Korean 試驗 — 試 'try/test' + 驗 'examine', literally 'a trial examination'. The collocation English speakers must memorize is 시험을 보다 — Koreans 'see' an exam, they do not 'do' it, so 시험을 하다 is wrong. Passing and failing are vivid metaphors with the particle 에: 시험에 붙다 (literally 'stick to the exam') = pass, 시험에 떨어지다 ('fall off the exam') = fail — note these take 에, not 을. Contrast 시험 with 퀴즈(quiz, a small in-class test) and with 검사(檢査, an inspection/medical test like 건강 검사): a graded school test is always 시험, never 퀴즈 unless it is a tiny informal one. The classic 직역 trap is 'take an exam' → 시험을 가지다/취하다 ✗ (English 'take' never transfers); and learners often write 시험을 통과하다, which is understandable but bookish — the everyday word is 붙다.
시험.explanation: 시험 (siheom) = "exam". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 시험을 보다 ("take an exam") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 시험, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.
시험.shortExplanation: 시험 means "exam" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 시험을 하다 instead of 시험을 보다. Koreans 'see/look at' an exam (보다); 하다 does not collocate with 시험.
Using 를 for pass/fail: 시험을 붙다 ✗. The verbs 붙다/떨어지다 take 에 — 시험에 붙다/떨어지다.
Translating 'take the exam' as 시험을 가지다 ('have/hold'). English 'take' is not literal here; the only natural verb is 보다.

usagePhrases.note: Fixed verb is 보다 (literally 'see'), never 하다
Existence/scheduling; the exam is the subject, so 이
붙다 'stick' = pass, 떨어지다 'fall' = fail; both take 에
기말(期末) = end of term; cf. 중간 시험 = midterm

examples.en: Is there an exam tomorrow?
examples.note: Casual; 있어요 used for a scheduled event existing

examples.en: I took the Korean exam yesterday.
examples.note: 봤어요 = past of 보다; the set phrase 시험을 보다

examples.en: I studied hard so I passed the exam.
examples.note: Pass = 시험에 붙다; note the particle is 에, not 를

ex.en: I studied every day during the preparation period.
ex.note: 기간 names the period; 동안 marks what happens through it.

기간.nuance: 기간 is Sino-Korean 期間 (期 'a fixed term/appointed time' + 間 'interval') — a defined stretch of time with a clear START and END, such as an exam season, a vacation, a contract term, or a sale window. Contrast it sharply with 시간 時間: 시간 is generic 'time/hours/duration' you measure (세 시간 = three hours), while 기간 is a bounded named span you don't usually count in hours (시험 기간 = the exam period, not '×N hours'). Also distinguish 동안, which is the grammatical word for 'during/for' and attaches to spans (방학 동안), whereas 기간 is the noun naming the span itself (often combined: 방학 기간 동안). 기간 collocates with administrative life — 접수/신청 기간 (application period), 계약/임대 기간 (contract/lease term), 유효 기간 (validity period/expiry), 공사 기간 — and takes 에 ('within') or 동안 ('throughout'). The English-speaker pitfall: translating every 'time' as 시간 and saying ✗시험 시간이 길어요 to mean 'the exam season is long' — that actually reads as 'the exam's duration (one sitting) is long'; the season is 시험 기간.
기간.explanation: 기간 (gigan) = "period". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 시험 기간 ("exam period") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 기간, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
기간.shortExplanation: 기간 means "period" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 시간 for a bounded span: ✗계약 시간 → ✓계약 기간, because a contract has a term (기간), not a clock-duration (시간).
Saying ✗기간이 걸려요 for 'it takes time' — taking time is 시간이 걸려요; 기간 names a fixed span and doesn't go with 걸리다.
Confusing 'how long is the period' (기간) with 'how much time' (시간): 유효 기간이 언제까지예요? (until when is it valid) vs 시간이 얼마나 걸려요? (how long does it take).

usagePhrases.note: 시험 기간이 길어요 = the exam period is long
방학 기간에 여행해요 = travel during the break
계약 기간은 일 년이에요 = the term is one year
할인 기간을 놓쳤어요 = I missed the sale window

examples.en: The application period ended.
examples.note: Official-notice tone; 접수 = receiving applications

examples.en: I learned a lot in a short period.
examples.note: 짧다 → 짧은; 기간 takes 에 to mean 'within that span'

examples.en: The road is blocked during the construction period.
examples.note: 기간 동안 = 'for the duration of'; everyday signage Korean

ex.ko: 한국에 머무는 동안 많이 연습할 거예요.
ex.en: While I stay in Korea, I will practice a lot.
ex.note: 머무는 동안 uses the verb modifier form.

머물다.nuance: 머물다 means to stay or remain somewhere for a stretch of time — a hotel, a friend's house, a city — and figuratively for a feeling or gaze that lingers (마음에 머물다). It is a ㄹ-stem (ㄹ-탈락) verb, the trap that trips up English speakers most: the ㄹ silently drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ, giving 머뭅니다 and the polite request 머무세요, while the 어-form irregularly doubles to 머물러요 / 머물렀어요. The synonym boundary: 묵다 is the close cousin specifically for lodging overnight (호텔에서 묵다) and feels a touch more colloquial for 'put up at'; 있다 ('be/stay') is what casual travel talk actually uses — 호텔에 있어요 — while 머물다 sounds a bit more composed or written. Place takes 에, and a duration like 며칠 or 일주일 sits bare with no particle. The pitfall is regularizing the conjugation: not 머물습니다 and not 머물어요.
머물다.explanation: "to stay" in Korean is 머물다 (meomulda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 머물러요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 머물다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 호텔에 머물다 ("to stay at a hotel") — then reshape the same stem into 머물고 싶어요 (desire), 머물 수 있어요 (ability), and 머물 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
머물다.shortExplanation: 머물다 means "to stay" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 머물다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 머물러요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing the formal form as 머물습니다 — the ㄹ drops before -ㅂ니다, so it is 머뭅니다.
Forgetting the 어-form doubles: it is 머물러요 / 머물렀어요, not 머물어요 / 머물었어요.
Putting a particle on the duration: say 며칠 머물러요, not 며칠을 머물러요 — the time span stands bare.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 머물다 becomes 머물 수 있어요 ("can") and 머물 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem
conjugationTips.body: 머물다 has an irregular stem (ㄹ). Memorize its polite form 머물러요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

usagePhrases.note: 에 marks the place of stay; the classic travel/lodging collocation.

examples.en: I'm staying in Seoul for a few days.
examples.note: Simple; 며칠 (a few days) sits with no particle.

examples.ko: 이번 출장 때는 친구 집에 머물렀어요.
examples.romanization: ibeon chuljang ttaeneun chingu jibe meomulleosseoyo.
examples.en: This business trip I stayed at a friend's place.
examples.note: Everyday; note the 어-form past 머물렀어요 (double 러).

examples.en: Tourists usually stay about a week.
examples.note: Real-situation, formal 합쇼체: the ㄹ drops before -ㅂ니다 → 머뭅니다.

ex.en: I will travel during vacation.
ex.note: A common period noun before 동안.

방학.nuance: 방학 is Sino-Korean 放學 — 放 'release/let go' + 學 'studies', literally 'releasing (from) studies', i.e. the official school break between terms (summer/winter). The crucial contrast is 방학 vs 휴가(休暇, 'leave/holiday'): 방학 belongs to the school calendar and applies to students/teachers, while 휴가 is the time off a worker takes from a job — a salaried adult on vacation is 휴가 중, never 방학 중. Also distinguish 방학 (a scheduled school break) from 휴일(休日, a single day off / public holiday like a national holiday) and 연휴(連休, a string of consecutive holidays). Note 방학을 하다 means '(the school) goes on break / break starts', an event, not 'I take a vacation'. The English-speaker pitfall is calling a working adult's trip 방학 (it must be 휴가), and forgetting that 'during vacation' uses the time particle 에 (방학에) or the duration noun 동안 (방학 동안), not 에서.
방학.explanation: 방학 (banghak) = "school vacation". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 방학에 ("during the break") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 방학, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.
방학.shortExplanation: 방학 means "school vacation" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 방학 for a working adult's time off — that is 휴가. 방학 is only the student/school-calendar break.
Saying 방학에서 for 'during vacation' ✗. A time period takes 에 (방학에) or 동안 (방학 동안); 에서 is for places/actions.
Confusing 방학 (a multi-week term break) with 휴일 (a single day off) or 연휴 (a holiday stretch).

usagePhrases.note: Time point/period takes 에: 방학에 여행하다
School 'goes on vacation'; 하다 here = the break begins
Season + 방학; cf. 겨울 방학 'winter break'
끝나다 = come to an end; subject takes 이

examples.en: When is the break?
examples.note: Simple schedule question; 이에요 = 'it is'

examples.en: I want to go to Korea during the break.
examples.note: 에 marks the time; -고 싶다 = 'want to'

examples.en: I worked a part-time job during the break.
examples.note: 동안 = 'for the duration of'; a very common time collocation

ex.en: My health got better.
ex.note: A core state-change sentence.

건강.nuance: 건강 is Sino-Korean 健康, where 健 means 'sturdy/robust' and 康 means 'peaceful/well,' together the sound, robust state of body and mind. It splits into a noun and an adjective: the noun 건강 ('health') pairs with 좋다/나쁘다 (good/bad) — never 높다/낮다 (high/low), which is the typical English-influenced slip from 'high level of health' — and you actively mind it with 챙기다 (건강을 챙기다, 'look after your health'); the adjective 건강하다 means 'to be healthy' (저는 건강해요 = 'I'm healthy'). Its honorific imperative 건강하세요 is a beloved set phrase, a warm farewell/blessing meaning 'stay healthy,' especially said to elders and at New Year. A near-synonym is 컨디션 (a loanword from 'condition') — but 컨디션 is your day-to-day fitness/energy level (오늘 컨디션이 안 좋아 = 'I'm not feeling great today'), whereas 건강 is your overall, long-term state of wellness; don't swap them.
건강.explanation: 건강 (geongang) = "health". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 건강이 좋아요 ("my health is good") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 건강, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.
건강.shortExplanation: 건강 means "health" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 건강이 높아요 for good health: health is 좋다/나쁘다, so it must be 건강이 좋아요.
Confusing 건강 with 컨디션: long-term wellness is 건강; today's energy/feeling is 컨디션.
Saying 건강이세요 instead of 건강하세요: the blessing comes from the adjective 건강하다, giving 건강하세요.

usagePhrases.note: 좋다, not 높다, describes good health
챙기다 = take care of, mind one's health

examples.en: Health is the most important thing.
examples.note: Simple: 건강이 + adjective, the core 'health is X' frame.

examples.ko: 요즘 운동을 시작해서 건강이 많이 좋아졌어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum undongeul sijakaeseo geongangi mani joajyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I started exercising lately, so my health has improved a lot.
examples.note: Everyday: 운동을 시작하다 + 건강이 좋아지다 (improve).

examples.en: Grandma, please always stay healthy and live a long, long life.
examples.note: Real-situation: honorific 건강하시다 + 사세요 as a warm blessing.

ex.en: The purpose of coming to Korea is study.
ex.note: Names the idea behind 위해서 sentences.

목적.nuance: 목적 (目的, '目 eye + 的 target' — the target your eye is fixed on) is the conscious aim or intention behind an action, more deliberate and goal-directed than 이유 (the reason behind it) or 원인 (the cause that produced it). Compare the near-synonym 목표: 목표 is a concrete, often measurable target you aim to hit (this month's sales 목표, a finish-line 목표), while 목적 is the underlying purpose or 'what it is for' — a company's 목적 may be 'to help people' but its 목표 is 'sell 1000 units'. Register leans formal/written: it dominates immigration forms (방문 목적), reports, and mission statements. Two pitfalls: do not pair it with 하다 (you 이루다/달성하다 a 목적, you never 목적을 하다), and do not confuse 목적 (purpose) with 목적지 (目的地, 'purpose-place' — the destination, an actual place).
목적.explanation: 목적 (mokjeok) means "purpose, goal". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 여행 목적 ("purpose of travel"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 목적 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
목적.shortExplanation: 목적 means "purpose, goal" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't confuse 목적 (purpose, abstract) with 목적지 (destination, a physical place you travel to) — adding 지(地, 'place') changes the meaning entirely.
Use 이루다/달성하다 with 목적, not 하다: 목적을 이루다 ('achieve a purpose'), never 목적을 하다.
Don't use 목적 where 목표 fits: a numeric/concrete target ('my goal is to lose 5 kg') is 목표, while 목적 is the broader 'what it is for'.

usagePhrases.note: fixed phrase on immigration/visa forms; also 방문 목적 = purpose of visit
the right verb is 이루다 (accomplish) or 달성하다, never 하다
describes an intended aim behind an action; 뚜렷한 목적이 있다 = have a clear aim
Verb-는 것이 목적이다 states what the aim is

examples.en: What's the purpose of this gathering?

examples.ko: 이 프로그램의 목적은 외국인을 돕는 것이에요.

ex.en: As I exercised, my habits changed.
ex.note: The noun that names the lifestyle change.

습관.nuance: 습관 (習慣, 習 'to practice/learn' + 慣 'to grow accustomed') frames a habit as something drilled in until it feels natural, and it leans slightly formal and neutral. The key contrast is 습관 vs 버릇: 습관 is a broad, often deliberate routine (early rising, daily exercise, good study habits), while 버릇 is colloquial and usually a quirky or annoying unconscious tic — nail-biting, leg-shaking, a child's bad manners. Crucially, scolding a child you say 버릇없다 ('has no manners / is rude'), never 습관없다. Both pair with 고치다 ('fix') for breaking them and 들이다/생기다 for forming them (습관을 들이다 = cultivate a habit; 습관이 생기다 = a habit forms). To say you have one, use 습관이 있다. Pitfall: English 'I have a habit of doing X' must use the verb's -는 present-modifier form before 습관: 일찍 자는 습관 (the habit of sleeping early), not 일찍 자기 습관. Also do not use 가지다 here — habits 있다/되다/생기다, they are not 'had' with 가지다.
습관.explanation: 습관 (seupgwan) means "habit". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 이것은 좋은 습관이에요. ("This is a good habit."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 습관 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
습관.shortExplanation: 습관 means "habit" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Forming 'have a habit of ~ing' wrongly: 운동하기 습관 is broken. Use the -는 modifier: 운동하는 습관이 있어요.
Using 습관 for a child's rudeness. 'That kid is rude/ill-mannered' is 그 아이는 버릇이 없어요, not 습관이 없어요.
Saying 습관을 가지고 있어요 by translating 'have a habit'. The idiomatic verb is 있다 or 되다: 습관이 있어요 / 습관이 됐어요.

usagePhrases.note: 좋은/나쁜 + 습관 describes the quality of a habit

usagePhrases.en: I want to fix a bad habit.
usagePhrases.note: 습관을 고치다 = 'correct/break a habit'; 고치다 = repair
습관이 되다 = 'turn into a habit', now automatic

usagePhrases.en: I have a habit of going to bed early.
usagePhrases.note: verb + -는 + 습관이 있다 = 'have the habit of ~ing'

examples.en: I have a habit of exercising every morning.
examples.note: -는 습관이 있다 is the frame for stating any routine

examples.en: I changed my coffee-drinking habit.
examples.note: 습관을 바꾸다 = 'change a habit' (swap it), milder than 고치다

examples.en: I can't break my nail-biting habit.
examples.note: Here a small bad tic is a 버릇, not 습관 — note the register difference
